docs.title: Helicopters
docs.text:
This page is the reference for helicopter emissions in OpenALAQS: the FOCA 2015 method, the helicopter catalog, and the trajectory that places the emissions in space. It is for modellers who need to know how helicopter movements are computed or who want to add a helicopter type.

  • FOCA 2015 method
  • Helicopter categories
  • Default catalog
  • What is not computed for helicopters
  • Trajectory parameters
  • Approach geometry
  • Departure geometry
  • Adding a new category

Primary reference:

Rindlisbacher T., Chabbey L., "Guidance on the Determination of Helicopter Emissions", Swiss Federal Office of Civil Aviation (FOCA), Edition 2, December 2015. Ref: COO.2207.111.2.2015750.

Cited below as FOCA 2015. Section and appendix references are to that document unless stated otherwise.

docs.title: FOCA 2015 method
docs.text:
Helicopter movements use the same Movements table as fixed-wing aircraft. The aircraft field holds an ICAO type designator (or a variant label, see Default catalog). Each identifier is first looked up in the helicopter catalog (default_helicopter); a match is computed as a helicopter, otherwise the fixed-wing catalog (default_aircraft) is used. No flag in the Movements table marks a helicopter: the lookup decides.

Emissions are computed live with the FOCA 2015 method from each helicopter's engine type, maximum shaft horsepower, engine count and category, for the FOCA LTO modes (ground idle, take-off, climb-out, approach). No precomputed emission indices are stored. The FOCA path is the same whatever the Method selected on the Configuration tab (Bymode or BFFM2).

FOCA gives no SOx. OpenALAQS computes it as the mode fuel times 0.758 g/kg for turboshaft engines (jet fuel) or 0.2 g/kg for piston engines (AvGas), the fuel sulphur values of Aircraft emissions: particulate matter.

The mode masses are then placed along a helicopter trajectory (see Trajectory parameters): ground idle as a point at the take-off or touchdown spot, the active mode along the flight path, cut at the LTO ceiling (the hour's mixing height, see Aircraft emissions) and the grid. The share of the active mode's time spent below the ceiling and inside the grid scales its FOCA mass.

Two inconsistencies of the FOCA 2015 PDF were resolved during implementation: the leading coefficient of the piston fuel flow, and the Appendix C power settings of the twin-heavy category. For the latter, Appendix C lists values that pre-date the 2015 update (legacy 2009-era values remained in the MODEL column despite text updates); OpenALAQS uses the post-2015 corrected values (Table 4).

In the code: open_alaqs/core/tools/foca_heli.py (fuel flow and emission index formulas; the "Known FOCA 2015 PDF inconsistencies" docstring), foca_heli_utils.compute_lto (mode masses), foca_heli_trajectory.active_mode_retained (cut at the ceiling and the grid), fuel_sulphur.py (SOx).

docs.title: Helicopter categories
docs.text:
Each movement is classified at run time into one of the four FOCA 2015 categories (section 2.4) from engine type, engine count and MTOM. The category is not stored.

Category Rule PISTON engine_type = PISTON SINGLE_TURBOSHAFT engine_type = TURBOSHAFT, one engine TWIN_TURBOSHAFT_LIGHT engine_type = TURBOSHAFT, two or more engines, MTOM ≤ 3400 kg TWIN_TURBOSHAFT_HEAVY engine_type = TURBOSHAFT, two or more engines, MTOM > 3400 kg

The 3400 kg threshold is defined in FOCA 2015 section 2.4. A twin turboshaft without MTOM cannot be classified and is rejected. The category drives both the emission formulas and the trajectory geometry.

In the code: derive_category in open_alaqs/core/tools/foca_heli.py.

docs.title: Default catalog
docs.text:
The catalog has 60 helicopter rows in default_helicopter, covering common types (ICAO codes R22, A109, EC35, AS32, S76, S92 and others), and 86 engine rows in default_helicopter_engines, covering the corresponding turboshaft and piston engines.

Table Field Notes default_helicopter icao ICAO type designator variant_label Distinguishes several rows per ICAO (e.g. A109E_POWER and A109II). The logical key is (icao, variant_label). manufacturer, name Free text mtow_kg Maximum take-off weight in kilograms (used for the category) engine_count Number of engines (used for the category) engine, engine_name Reference a row of default_helicopter_engines max_shp_per_engine Maximum shaft horsepower per engine is_default 1 for the default variant of the ICAO code default_helicopter_engines engine_name Logical key engine_full_name Free text engine_type PISTON or TURBOSHAFT max_shp_per_engine Used when the helicopter row does not give one source Provenance citation

The Movements table has no variant_label column. Its aircraft column takes either an ICAO code (the default variant is used) or a variant_label (that row is used). When an identifier matches both an ICAO code and a variant label, the ICAO code wins.

To add a helicopter type, insert a row into default_helicopter that references an existing engine of default_helicopter_engines (or insert the engine row first). The minimum fields are icao, variant_label, mtow_kg, engine_count, engine, engine_name, max_shp_per_engine and is_default. Movements whose aircraft matches the new row are then computed with the FOCA method.

docs.title: What is not computed for helicopters
docs.text:
• APU, GSE, GPU and main engine start. None are computed for helicopters, whatever apu_code and gate_emissions_code say. The gate calculation is not run for a helicopter movement: the gate is only the helipad, the origin of the trajectory. Helicopters have no taxi route; the helicopter taxi step adds ground idle only. The FOCA 2015 LTO cycle covers ground idle, take-off, climb-out, approach and landing on its own, so nothing is counted twice.
  • Above the LTO ceiling. The helicopter trajectory ends at 3000 ft above ground (ICAO LTO definition) and is cut at the hour's mixing height when that is lower; emissions above are not modelled.

In the code: MovementSourceModule.process skips the gate calculator for helicopters; TaxiingEmissionCalculator._apply_taxiing_emissions_for_helicopters adds ground idle.

docs.title: Trajectory parameters
docs.text:
The trajectory generator builds the 3D geometry of a helicopter LTO from the per-category parameters below. The four categories are those of Helicopter categories. Fuel flow, emission indices and mode masses are not trajectory parameters: they come from the FOCA 2015 method. The trajectory times are used only to cut the active mode at the LTO ceiling and the grid.

In the code: TRAJECTORY_PARAMS in open_alaqs/core/tools/foca_heli_trajectory.py.

docs.title: Global constants
docs.text: symbol value source LTO_CEILING_FT 3000 ft AGL ICAO LTO cycle definition (Annex 16 Vol. II Appendix 3 §1.2) HOVER_ALT_FT 5 ft AGL FOCA Appendix A (hover IGE altitude convention) HOVER_DURATION_S 18 s FOCA Appendix A (assumed universal across categories) Twin-turboshaft MTOM threshold 3400 kg FOCA §2.4

docs.title: PISTON
docs.text:
Representative airframe: Robinson R22. Selected as the canonical piston single because it dominates the FOCA fleet sample and its performance is published in the R22 Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH) in matching units.

field value source climb_roc_fpm 500 R22 POH §4 (normal climb rate at sea-level ISA) climb_tas_kt 60 R22 POH §4 (Vy, best rate of climb speed) cruise_tas_kt 75 R22 POH §5 (75% MCP cruise TAS at 4000 ft) approach_tas_initial_kt 60 Operational convention (Vy is used as the approach entry speed for piston helicopters per FOCA Appendix A) approach_tas_final_kt 30 Operational convention (slow-down to translational-lift speed before hover) approach_rod_initial_fpm 500 Symmetric with climb ROC; FOCA Appendix A descent profile approach_rod_final_fpm 250 Reduced ROD for final segment; FOCA Appendix A descent profile approach_start_nm 5.0 Distance at which descent from LTO ceiling commences. FOCA Appendix A. Not used by the generator (see Approach geometry).

docs.title: SINGLE_TURBOSHAFT
docs.text:
The FOCA 2015 reference table is specified for this category directly.

field value source climb_roc_fpm 1000 FOCA Appendix A climb_tas_kt 60 FOCA Appendix A cruise_tas_kt 120 FOCA §2.1 worked example approach_tas_initial_kt 60 FOCA Appendix A "DCT" (descent) row approach_tas_final_kt 30 FOCA Appendix A approach_rod_initial_fpm 700 FOCA Appendix A approach_rod_final_fpm 250 FOCA Appendix A approach_start_nm 5.0 FOCA Appendix A. Not used by the generator (see Approach geometry).

docs.title: TWIN_TURBOSHAFT_LIGHT
docs.text:
Twin turboshaft helicopters with MTOM ≤ 3400 kg. Representative airframes include the Eurocopter EC135, AS355, BO105. FOCA 2015 does not publish a separate trajectory table for this category; the values below are obtained by scaling up from SINGLE_TURBOSHAFT in proportion to the typical performance ratio observed across the representative airframes (flight manuals: EC135 §4-5, AS355 §4-5).

field value source climb_roc_fpm 1500 Scaled from FOCA Appendix A SINGLE_TURBOSHAFT; corroborated against EC135 P2 flight manual §4-5 (sea-level Vy ROC, AUW 2720 kg) climb_tas_kt 80 EC135 / AS355 flight manuals (Vy at AUW representative for light twin) cruise_tas_kt 150 EC135 / AS355 flight manuals (recommended cruise TAS, sea-level, ISA) approach_tas_initial_kt 80 Symmetric with climb_tas_kt (FOCA Appendix A convention) approach_tas_final_kt 40 Operational convention (final approach to hover; faster than single because of higher disk loading) approach_rod_initial_fpm 700 FOCA Appendix A initial descent ROD (unchanged across light categories) approach_rod_final_fpm 300 Scaled from SINGLE_TURBOSHAFT final ROD approach_start_nm 6.0 Slightly longer than single because of higher initial TAS (descent angle preserved). Not used by the generator (see Approach geometry).

docs.title: TWIN_TURBOSHAFT_HEAVY
docs.text:
Twin turboshaft helicopters with MTOM > 3400 kg. The reference airframe is the AS332L1 Super Puma (MTOM 8600 kg), for which a complete technical data set is published in the AS332L1 Pilot's Operating Manual. FOCA 2015 documents the methodology for this category but uses single-turboshaft performance values in its worked example; this implementation uses heavy-twin values to avoid under-estimating LTO duration at large airframes.

The FOCA mode power settings of this category are discussed in FOCA 2015 method.

field value source climb_roc_fpm 1920 AS332L1 Technical Data, ROC at AUW 8000 kg, climb at Vy 70 kt climb_tas_kt 70 AS332L1 Technical Data Vy cruise_tas_kt 139 AS332L1 Technical Data recommended cruise TAS at 8000 kg approach_tas_initial_kt 70 Symmetric with climb_tas_kt approach_tas_final_kt 40 Operational convention (final approach to hover) approach_rod_initial_fpm 700 FOCA Appendix A initial descent ROD approach_rod_final_fpm 300 Operational convention approach_start_nm 7.0 Longer approach distance scales with cruise TAS (descent angle preserved at ~3°). Not used by the generator (see Approach geometry).

docs.title: Approach geometry
docs.text:
The arrival fills the FOCA approach time (5.5 min):

  1. a level segment at the LTO ceiling at approach_tas_initial_kt, when the two descents take less than the approach time;
  2. a descent at approach_tas_initial_kt and approach_rod_initial_fpm to 500 ft AGL;
  3. a final descent at approach_tas_final_kt and approach_rod_final_fpm to hover (5 ft AGL).

When the two descents take longer than the approach time, both are shortened in proportion: the arrival still starts at the LTO ceiling, the break between the two descents moves up (PISTON about 1030 ft, SINGLE_TURBOSHAFT about 520 ft instead of 500 ft) and the final descent is steeper than approach_rod_final_fpm. The arrival then starts about 8.7 km (PISTON), 8.4 km (SINGLE_TURBOSHAFT), 11.5 km (TWIN_TURBOSHAFT_LIGHT) and 10.4 km (TWIN_TURBOSHAFT_HEAVY) from the touchdown spot. approach_start_nm is not used by the generator. Hover is held for HOVER_DURATION_S (18 s) before touchdown.

In the code: build_arrival and FINAL_BREAK_ALT_FT in foca_heli_trajectory.py.

docs.title: Departure geometry
docs.text:
Ground idle at the origin for 80 % of the GI time, hover for HOVER_DURATION_S at HOVER_ALT_FT, then climb at climb_tas_kt and climb_roc_fpm until the LTO ceiling (3000 ft AGL) or the end of the FOCA take-off time (PISTON stops at about 2000 ft); any remaining take-off time is flown level at cruise_tas_kt.

The origin is the centroid of the movement's gate (helipad), else the runway end; arrivals approach from the approach side along the runway heading. Ground idle after landing is 20 % of the GI time.

In the code: build_departure in foca_heli_trajectory.py; runway_alignment_for_helicopter in open_alaqs/core/GeoTransformation.py.

docs.title: Adding a new category
docs.text:
What to change in the code for a new FOCA category is in CODE_FLOW.md.

See also: Aircraft emissions, Reference data, User Guide: movements, Input formats: movements.

docs.title: OpenALAQS reference data
docs.text:
This page describes the default data that ships with OpenALAQS: the tables of the study database, where their values come from, and where their provenance is recorded. It is for modellers who want to check or update the default emission factors; the methods that use these tables are described on the method pages linked from each section.

  • OpenALAQS database
  • Aircraft and airport data
  • Aircraft engine emission indices
  • APU, main engine start and ground support equipment
  • Helicopters
  • ANP flight profiles
  • COPERT road vehicle emission factors
  • Stationary source emission factors
  • Emission dynamics

docs.title: OpenALAQS database
docs.text:
The internal OpenALAQS database contains default emission factors for all airport sources. When the user creates a new study, these files are copied to the new .alaqs file. The study keeps its copy: a study made with an older version keeps the older tables until they are refreshed (see Upgrading from 5.3.x). If the user has access to more up-to-date information, they can update the default data as described in the README file.

Alternatively, OpenALAQS files can be easily viewed and edited with DB Browser for SQLite an open source tool designed for manipulating SQLite database files.

docs.title: Aircraft and airport data
docs.text:
The internal database contains an extensive list of aircraft (see default_aircraft) along with information on the most representative engine, APU, departure/arrival profiles and other characteristics.

A list of airports is also available (see default_airports) with information on their location and elevation (feet above mean sea level).

docs.title: Aircraft engine emission indices
docs.text:
Aircraft emissions are calculated based on the recommendations of ICAO Doc. 9889. The methods are described in Aircraft emissions.

Information on exhaust emissions of aircraft engines is taken from the ICAO Aircraft Engine Emissions Databank (EEDB) and the FOCA Aircraft Piston Engine database. Default emission factors are also provided for some turboprop engine types; additional information can be obtained from the confidential FOI Turboprop Emissions Database.

docs.title: Engine emission index table (default_aircraft_engine_ei)
docs.text:
The engine EI table contains one row per engine per LTO mode (TX, AP, CL, TO). The key columns are:

Column Description engine_name ICAO engine designator mode LTO mode: TX, AP, CL, TO fuel_kg_sec Reference fuel flow (kg/s per engine, SLS) nox_ei, co_ei, hc_ei EEDB gas-phase emission indices (g/kg) sox_ei SOx (as SO2) emission index (g/kg): 0.758 for the Jet Fuel rows and 0.2 for the AvGas rows of the shipped data; a 0 or empty value is replaced by the value of the row's fuel pm10_ei Total combustion PM10 EI (g/kg) = pm10_nonvol + pm10_sul + pm10_organic (to rounding), except for the FOCA pistons and turboprops (P, PF, T601 to T603, T717, T790; source "ACT_PRF 2.6.3 (CAEP14 FOCA 2026-10-09)"), whose pm10_ei is the FOCA total PM of the file: the file gives no volatile and sulphate parts for them, so they carry no pm10_sul and pm10_organic. For the FOCA business jets the file gives the parts: B004 and B134 take them (they sum to the file's total); for B601, B602 and B603 the file's parts do not sum to its total (0.84 to 1.60 times, by mode), and pm10_ei is the sum of the parts, nvPM + volatile + sulphate pm10_nonvol Non-volatile PM (nvPM) mass EI (g/kg) from ICAO EEDB pm10_sul Sulphate vPM EI (g/kg): a constant 0.04896 g/kg (48.96 mg/kg) for the Jet Fuel engines with PM data, 0 for the AvGas rows pm10_organic Organic vPM EI (g/kg), from the EEDB HC EI of the mode p1_ei, p2_ei PM1.0 and PM2.5 EI placeholders (g/kg); currently equal to pm10_ei nvpm_number_ei nvPM number EI (#/kg) from ICAO EEDB press_ratio Overall pressure ratio (OPR) for MEEM V1 above 3000 ft above the aerodrome: the ICAO EEDB v31 value, ACT_PRF for engines not in it; set for 890 jet engines, empty for the others (30 is then used) meem_nvpm_m_i_f00_avg Thrust of the 5th nvPM mass point for MEEM V1 (used when above 0, with nvpm_m_max_mgkg); same sources; above 0 for 77 engines (51 EEDB 5-point engines and 26 ACT_PRF 5-point engines), 0 for the 4-point engines nvpm_m_max_mgkg Maximum nvPM mass EI (mg/kg), same sources; the 5th mass point when meem_nvpm_m_i_f00_avg is above 0, otherwise not used meem_nvpm_n_i_f00_avg Thrust of the 5th nvPM number point for MEEM V1 (used when above 0, with nvpm_n_max_nkg); same sources as the mass point nvpm_n_max_nkg Maximum nvPM number EI (#/kg), same sources; the 5th number point when meem_nvpm_n_i_f00_avg is above 0, otherwise not used

How the PM columns are derived (sulphate and organic vPM, SOx from the fuel sulphur content, MEEM V1 above 3000 ft, brake wear) is described in Aircraft emissions: particulate matter. Columns that are no longer read are listed in DEPRECATIONS.md.

docs.title: APU, main engine start and ground support equipment
docs.text:
• APU emission factors and operating times: default_aircraft_apu_ef and default_apu_times. The APU model of each aircraft is the apu_id column of default_aircraft.
  • Main engine start (MES) emissions per aircraft group: default_aircraft_start_ef (unit gram/aircraft in the CSV, applied once per engine started).
  • GSE and GPU emission factors and activity times: default_gate_profiles. The emission factors are in grams of pollutant per hour, by gate type, aircraft category and operation type.

How these tables are used, and how the apu_code and gate_emissions_code fields of the movements switch them on, is described in Aircraft emissions: APU, GSE and engine start.

docs.title: Helicopters
docs.text: Helicopters have their own catalog (default_helicopter, default_helicopter_engines) and no stored emission indices: emissions are computed with the FOCA 2015 method. See Helicopters.

docs.title: ANP flight profiles
docs.text:
The Aircraft Noise and Performance (ANP) database contains a standardized dataset with information related to aircraft flight performance under various conditions. This includes engine performance characteristics and flight profiles for a wide variety of aircraft types, including standard departure and approach procedures.

We note that in the context of EASA having a legal mandate to collect and verify the ANP data since Reg. (EU) 598/2014 has entered into force, the management and hosting of the ANP legacy data (version 2.3 and prior versions) have been transferred from EUROCONTROL to EASA in order to establish a single ANP data source.

OpenALAQS stores the ANP fixed-point profiles in default_aircraft_profiles. Each profile is a series of points with horizontal and vertical distance, true airspeed, power setting and LTO mode. Profiles with course = CUSTOM are not ANP profiles: they hold trajectories derived from ADS-B recordings. The sources of the catalogue and the corrections made to it are recorded in AIRCRAFT_PROFILES_PROVENANCE.md. How the profiles are placed on the runway and used in the emission calculation is described in Aircraft emissions: flight profiles (ANP).

docs.title: COPERT road vehicle emission factors
docs.text:
The roadway and parking emission factors (landside, airside and parking lots) come from COPERT (version 5.4.52), the EU standard vehicle emissions calculator, developed by EMISIA for the European Environment Agency (EEA).

COPERT contains emission factors for more than 450 individual vehicle types considering factors such as vehicle type, age, mileage, and driving conditions. Its methodology comprises the road transport chapters in the EMEP/EEA Air Emissions Inventory Guidebook and is consistent with the 2006 IPCC Guidelines.

The vehicle categories in the OpenALAQS table are Passenger Cars (PCs), Light Commercial Vehicles (LCVs), Heavy Duty Trucks (HDTs), buses and motorcycles. Only petrol and diesel engines are included. Emission factors are provided for 38 entries: 26 EU Member States (Slovakia is not currently present in the dataset), the EU27 and EU28 aggregates, plus UK, Iceland, Norway, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, North Macedonia, Turkey, Albania, Serbia, and Montenegro.

Special remarks:

  • HDTs petrol: only "Conventional" Euro standard option is available.
  • Motorcycles: only "Petrol" fuel option is available.
  • Buses: only "Diesel" fuel option is available.
  • Evaporative emissions: only VOC pollutant is available.
  • The emission factors include information for idling periods.

The values are in default_vehicle_ef_copert5, with separate rows for Hot, Cold and Evaporation conditions and one column per 10 km/h speed bin from 10 to 130 km/h. Two data items are open:

  • EU27 / EU28 labelling mismatch: the EU27 country aggregate is missing PM10 rows (EU28 has them instead). Correcting it requires re-running the ingest to produce a consistent EU-aggregate set.
  • NH3 values appear about 10 times lower than the Guidebook Tier 2 references. This has no effect on results because NH3 is not an output of the road traffic calculation.

The file layout, the source COPERT version and these data items are documented in DATASET_PROVENANCE.md. How the factors become fleet-averaged emission factors and hourly emissions is described in Stationary and road sources: road traffic and parkings.

docs.title: Stationary source emission factors
docs.text:
default_stationary_ef holds the default emission factors of point sources, by category and type. The seven categories are Other (0), Incinerator (1), Power/Heat Plant (2), Fuel Tank (3), Solvent Degreaser (4), Surface Coating (5) and Stationary IC Engine (6). The main columns are:

Column Description category, type, description Source category, type within the category, and its name co_kg_k, hc_kg_k, nox_kg_k, sox_kg_k, particulate_kg_k, p1_kg_k, p2_kg_k Emission factors in kg per activity unit activity_unit Unit the factors refer to: 1000_m3 (natural gas), 1000_L (liquid fuel throughput), 1000_kg (waste, coating), hr (engine operating hours) reference Source of the factors: US EPA AP-42 (sections 1.4, 3.3 and 3.4) or EMEP/EEA (1.A.4); AP-42 (legacy mapping) for the rows carried over from earlier versions deprecated 1 for the legacy rows kept so that older studies still resolve, 0 for the current rows recommended_hour_profile, recommended_day_profile, recommended_month_profile Suggested activity profile names for the type

The shipped table has 64 rows, 14 of them current. The factors can be modified if more up-to-date information is available. The calculation is described in Stationary and road sources: point and area sources.

docs.title: Emission dynamics
docs.text:
default_emission_dynamics holds the source dynamics parameters per aircraft group and LTO mode: horizontal extent, vertical extent and vertical shift, once for the default method and once for the smooth & shift method (columns ending in _sas). The values were originally derived from LASPORT v1.6 and later updated to LASPORT v2.2. Their use is described in Stationary and road sources: source dynamics.

See also: Aircraft emissions, Stationary and road sources, Helicopters, Dataset provenance (COPERT).

docs.title: Stationary and road sources: emission methods
docs.text:
This page explains how OpenALAQS computes the emissions of road traffic, parkings, point sources, area sources and engine test sites, and how source dynamics (Smooth & Shift) give aircraft emissions a volume. It is for modellers who want to know what the numbers mean; how to enter these sources in QGIS is in the User Guide.

  • Road traffic and parkings (COPERT)
  • Point and area sources
  • Engine test sites
  • Source dynamics (Smooth and Shift)
  • References

docs.title: Road traffic and parkings (COPERT)
docs.text:
Roadway emissions (landside and airside) and parking emissions are based on the COPERT 5 emission factors and the road transport chapters of the EMEP/EEA Air Emissions Inventory Guidebook. The emission factor data and its provenance are described in Reference data: COPERT.

The implementation preserves the core information of COPERT, with some simplification tailored to the scope of OpenALAQS. It generates typical emission factors for roadway segments or parking areas based on fleet year (as a proxy for Euro standard), country, fleet mix, number of vehicles, temperature, average speed, and roadway segment length.

The calculation has two stages: the fleet-averaged emission factors are computed when the user saves a roadway or parking (the Recalculate button), and the emission masses are computed for each hour when emissions are calculated.

docs.title: Stage 1: fleet-averaged emission factors
docs.text:
This is the Tier 3 method of the Guidebook. The module and its tables (3-39 to 3-46) follow the EMEP/EEA Guidebook 2019, Update Oct. 2020; later additions cite the Guidebook 2023, Update 2025.

  1. Emission factor lookup. The row of default_vehicle_ef_copert5 is selected for the country of the study and the tabulated speed closest to the feature's speed (rounded to the nearest 10 km/h between 10 and 130 km/h). Separate rows exist for Hot, Cold and Evaporation conditions.

  2. Hot emissions. For each technology (vehicle category × fuel × Euro standard), the hot emission factor e_hot [g/km] is read from the table: 

    E_hot [g] = N_vehicles × M [km] × e_hot [g/km]
    where M is fixed at 1 000 km per vehicle. It is a normalisation that cancels in step 4; the actual distance is applied in Stage 2.

  3. Cold-start emissions. The cold mileage fraction β follows EMEP/EEA Table 3-39: 

    β = 0.6474 − 0.02545 × L − (0.00974 − 0.000385 × L) × T
    where L is the average trip length, always 12.4 km (a default, not country-specific), and T is the ambient temperature [°C] of the study setup. For diesel HDTs and buses a separate formula applies: β = min(8.25 / L, 1) (EMEP/EEA Guidebook 2023 Update 2025, chapter 1.A.3.b.i-iv §3.4, p.77). Motorcycles and petrol HDTs use β = 0 (hot emissions only).

A pollutant-specific reduction factor bc (EMEP/EEA Tables 3-41, 3-43, 3-46) modifies β for Euro 2 to Euro 6 petrol passenger cars and LCVs and for Euro 6 diesel passenger cars: 

E_cold [g] = N_vehicles × M [km] × β × bc × e_cold [g/km]

  1. Total and fleet average. E_total = E_hot + E_cold, summed across all technologies of the fleet mix: 

    e_avg [g/km] = Σ E_total [g] / Σ (N_vehicles × M [km])
    For a roadway, e_avg is the stored emission factor (co_gm_km, nox_gm_km, and so on, in g/km per vehicle).

  2. Parkings. A parking stores emission factors per vehicle (g/vehicle). Each pollutant is e_avg times the parking's Travel Distance (converted from m to km). VOC also receives the evaporative emission: the Evaporation rows (Diurnal and Hot soak; Running losses are excluded, see below) are summed into eVOC [g/day] per vehicle and scaled by the idle time: 

    VOC_evap [g/vehicle] = eVOC [g/day] × idle_time [min] / (24 × 60)
HC [g/vehicle]       = e_avg_VOC [g/km] × travel_distance [km] + VOC_evap [g/vehicle]

The temperature is the airport temperature of the study setup. The country and fleet year are also study settings.

In the code: open_alaqs/core/tools/copert5.py (roadway_emission_factors) and copert5_utils.py (ef_query, cold_mileage_fractions, calculate_evaporation).

docs.title: Stage 2: emissions per hour
docs.text:
For each hour, the activity of a roadway or parking is the number of vehicles in that hour: the Vehicles per Year spread over the year with the hourly, daily and monthly profiles, as for point sources (see Point and area sources).

Roadway: 

emission [kg] = EF [g/km] × L [km] × vehicles_in_hour × length_fraction / 1000
where L is the length of the roadway line, and length_fraction is 1 unless the roadway extends outside the calculation grid, in which case it is the share of its length inside the grid (the emission then gets the clipped geometry).

Parking: 

emission [kg] = EF [g/vehicle] × vehicles_in_hour / 1000

In the code: RoadwaySourceModule.process and ParkingSourceModule.process in open_alaqs/core/modules/.

docs.title: Pollutant mapping
docs.text:
OpenALAQS output column COPERT 5 source Notes co_kg eCO[g/km] Hot + cold hc_kg eVOC[g/km] + evaporation VOC used as HC proxy; evaporative VOC for parkings only nox_kg eNOx[g/km] Hot + cold sox_kg eSO2[g/km] Hot only pm10_kg ePM2.5[g/km] COPERT 5 reports PM2.5; used as PM10 p1_kg ePM0.1[g/km] PM0.1 from COPERT 5 p2_kg ePM2.5[g/km] Same as pm10_kg

PM10 equals PM2.5 for road transport exhaust (EMEP/EEA Guidebook 2023 Update 2025, §1.1, p.4). CO2 is not computed by the COPERT module: the co2_kg column stays zero for roadway and parking sources.

docs.title: Known limitations and future work
docs.text:
These are documented simplifications of the COPERT 5 implementation; comments in the code refer to them by number. They do not block correct use of the module.

1. Parking cold-start option. By default the cold-start part of a parking is the fleet-averaged factor (computed for a 12.4 km trip) times the short parking distance. An option, off by default and not set from the plugin forms, makes the parking carry the full cold-start emission of departing vehicles. It evaluates the cold factor at a single speed (30 km/h) over a single trip length (12.4 km). Per the Guidebook 2023 Update 2025 chapter 1.A.3.b.i-iv §3.4, cold-start factors depend on speed (Tables 3-40, 3-44, 3-47) and the trip length should reflect the actual trip-length distribution. Both values can be overridden per study (parking_cold_speed_kmh, parking_cold_trip_length_km).

2. Evaporation: Hot soak scaling and Running losses. Running losses are excluded from parking evaporation per Guidebook chapter 1.A.3.b.v §4.7 (p.28-29). Two approximations remain:

  • Hot soak per event: Diurnal and Hot soak are both scaled by idle_time / (24 × 60). Per Guidebook §2.1.3 and the Tier 2 equations, Hot soak is a fixed amount per parking event (one per engine turn-off). The approximation understates Hot soak for short parkings and overstates it for long ones.
  • Running losses on roadways: per Guidebook §4.7, Running losses depend on mileage and belong to driving sources. OpenALAQS does not add an evaporation contribution to roadways, so this VOC is not in the inventory (small on modern fleets).

3. Data items. The EU27 / EU28 labelling mismatch and the low NH3 values of the data file are described in Reference data: COPERT.

How the Guidebook is cited in the code, and what to re-check at the next Guidebook update, is in DATASET_PROVENANCE.md.

docs.title: Point and area sources
docs.text:
Point sources represent stationary facilities such as power and heating plants, incinerators, training fires, fuel storage tanks and stationary internal-combustion engines. Area sources hold user-defined emissions not covered by the other source types. Both use the same method: an emission factor times an annual activity, spread over the year with activity profiles.

  • Point source. The emission factors (kg per activity unit) come from the selected category and type in default_stationary_ef. The activity is Activity per Year in the source's Activity Unit (for example 1000_m3 of natural gas, 1000_L of fuel throughput, hr of engine operation, 1000_kg of waste).
  • Area source. The user enters the emission factors (kg per unit) and Units per Year.

For each hour h of the inventory year:

emission_kg(h) = EF_kg_per_unit × annual_activity / H
                 × hour_factor(h) × day_factor(h) × month_factor(h) / profile_mean

where H is the number of hours in the year (8760, or 8784 in a leap year) and profile_mean is the mean of the product of the three profile factors over the calendar year. Dividing by it makes the annual total exactly EF × annual_activity, whether or not the profiles average to 1. With all three profiles constant, each hour gets EF × annual_activity / H. For an interval of several hours, the hourly values are summed.

The profiles are therefore relative shapes, not absolute activity ratios. Their values are non-negative and not capped at 1; only the ratios within a profile matter. Two consequences:

  • A factor of 0 for some period (for example a night curfew) zeroes the emission in that period and moves its mass to the other periods: the annual total is kept. To lower the annual emission, lower the annual activity instead.
  • If every factor is 0 (profile_mean = 0), the emission is 0 in every hour; no normalisation is applied.

The same profile normalisation gives the hourly number of vehicles of roadways and parkings.

Worked examples (from the default factors):

  • Heating plant on natural gas (category 2): 850 000 m³ per year is Activity per Year = 850 with unit 1000_m3. With the type Natural Gas, EMEP Tier 1 commercial/institutional (nox_kg_k = 1.84), annual NOx = 850 × 1.84 = 1 564 kg.
  • Diesel backup generator (category 6, Stationary IC Engine): 400 operating hours per year with unit hr. With the type Diesel <600 hp, Uncontrolled (nox_kg_k = 4.41 kg/hr), annual NOx = 400 × 4.41 = 1 764 kg.

The fuel tank factors (category 3, unit 1000_L of throughput) give HC only: they are evaporative VOC losses.

Stationary IC engine types are diesel reciprocating engines at two power tiers, >600 hp (split into Prechamber and Open-Chamber combustion, per AP-42 §3.4) and <600 hp.

An area source flagged as an engine test site does not use this method; see Engine test sites.

In the code: SourceModule.getRelativeActivityPerHour (open_alaqs/core/interfaces/SourceModule.py), PointSourceModule.process, AreaSourceModule.process.

docs.title: Engine test sites
docs.text:
An engine test site (run-up pad) is an area source whose emissions come from discrete engine test events instead of an emission rate times a profile. Each event gives a start and end time, an aircraft type and engine, the running time in each of the four ICAO modes, and a thrust computation mode. The events file format is in Input formats.

For each event and each mode with a non-zero running time:

t_effective_s  = t_mode_s × engine_count × period_window_fraction
fuel_burned_kg = fuel_flow_kg_s × t_effective_s
mass_g         = EI_g_per_kg × fuel_burned_kg

period_window_fraction splits events that straddle two inventory periods: it is the share of the event's duration inside the period. An event from 09:30 to 10:30 with a 09:00 to 10:00 period gives 50 % of its emissions to that period and 50 % to the next. The mode times are treated as uniform over the event window.

Thrust computation modes (per event, default snap):

  • snap: the ICAO EEDB emission index of each mode, no ambient correction.
  • meem: the nvPM correction (MEEM V1). It gives the same result as snap for engine tests, because the test modes are the ICAO certification thrust settings at ground level.
  • bffm2: the gas-phase emission indices (NOx, CO, HC) are corrected with the ambient conditions of the meteo row nearest in time to the event's midpoint, ties to the earlier row; plugin and standalone use the same row (SAE AIR 5715, see Aircraft emissions: BFFM2). PM10 and SOx are taken from the engine table per mode (SOx 0.758 g/kg for jet fuel and 0.2 g/kg for AvGas when the table gives none). Without any meteo row, ISA conditions are used and a warning is written once per run.

Engine test sites are not processed as ordinary area sources, so they are not counted twice.

In the code: open_alaqs/core/modules/EngineTestSourceModule.py.

docs.title: Source dynamics (Smooth and Shift)
docs.text:
OpenALAQS calculates three-dimensional emission distributions. To feed them into dispersion models, the near-field exhaust dynamics must be accounted for: engine momentum, buoyant plume rise and atmospheric diffusion. Source dynamics approximate these effects by expanding each aircraft trajectory segment into a three-dimensional volume before it enters the emission grid.

The approach comes from the EUROCONTROL report EEC/SEE/2005/016 (Smooth & Shift) and was used to connect ALAQS-AV output to dispersion models. The parameters were originally derived from LASPORT v1.6 and later updated to LASPORT v2.2. They are stored in default_emission_dynamics per aircraft group and LTO mode and can be modified.

Source dynamics apply to aircraft movements: flight segments and taxiing get a volume. When source dynamics are on, gate emissions get a fixed vertical extent from 0 to 5 m. Roadways, parkings, point and area sources are not affected.

The figure below shows a taxiway example: each line segment (black) is expanded into a lateral and vertical polygon volume.

docs.title: Volume geometry
docs.text:
For each segment between two consecutive trajectory points, a cross-section is built from three parameters per aircraft group and LTO mode:

Parameter Column (default) Column (smooth & shift) Description d_h horizontal_extent_m horizontal_extent_m_sas Full lateral width of the volume [m], centred on the trajectory d_v vertical_extent_m vertical_extent_m_sas Vertical extent of the volume [m] s_v vertical_shift_m vertical_shift_m_sas Vertical shift of the volume [m] (used by default only)

The Source Dynamics option of the Configuration tab selects the method: none, default or smooth & shift.

none: no volume is built; the emissions stay on the trajectory.

default: the lower edge of the volume is the trajectory point shifted vertically by s_v, and the volume extends upward by d_v:

z_lower = z_trajectory + s_v
z_upper = z_lower + d_v

smooth & shift: the volume is centred on the trajectory point and spans d_v below and above it. The vertical shift column vertical_shift_m_sas is not used:

z_lower = z_trajectory − d_v
z_upper = z_trajectory + d_v

In both methods the polygon vertices are clamped to zero (ground level), but the vertical extent given to the emission record (z_min) is not: with a negative s_v or with smooth & shift near the ground, z_min can be below 0. Taxiing segments are at ground level (z = 0), and there is no horizontal shift: the volume is always centred laterally on the trajectory (the horizontal_shift_m column of the table is not read).

The figure below illustrates the two methods for a representative climb segment (JET LARGE, CL mode, training example dynamics):

In the code: GeoTransformation._compute_z_envelope and GeoTransformation.create_polygon_3d in open_alaqs/core/GeoTransformation.py; the parameters are read in open_alaqs/core/interfaces/EmissionDynamics.py.

docs.title: LTO mode and TO/CL reclassification
docs.text:
The LTO mode selects the row of default_emission_dynamics used for each segment. OpenALAQS follows a different convention from LASPORT:

  • LASPORT defines TO as the ground roll only; once the aircraft is airborne it is in CL.
  • OpenALAQS assigns TO through the entire take-off phase. A TO segment whose end point is above the ground (z₂ > 0) uses the CL dynamics for its volume. The LTO mode of the emission record is not changed; only the dynamics lookup is.

The volume therefore widens and deepens as soon as the aircraft leaves the ground, reflecting the change from ground roll to free-jet exhaust. The figure below shows this on a departure trajectory:

docs.title: Departure and approach trajectories
docs.text:
The figure below shows the volumes of a departure and an approach for a JET LARGE aircraft, with the dynamics of the training example, for both methods. The coloured bands are the vertical extent at each segment; the navy shading is the overall vertical envelope given to the emission record (z_min to z_max).

Observations:

  • With default, approach (AP) volumes are shifted down (s_v = −100 m for JET LARGE), representing the exhaust plume below the glide slope.
  • With smooth & shift, AP volumes are centred on the trajectory and extend d_v = 100 m above and below it.
  • With smooth & shift, the envelope of the full departure spans from the ground to well above 900 m.

docs.title: Parameter values
docs.text:
The figure below summarises d_h and d_v for the main aircraft groups and the four LTO modes under both methods. JET LARGE aircraft have the largest volumes; helicopters and GSE the smallest.

The complete table is default_emission_dynamics. Values for JET LARGE (the s_v of smooth & shift is stored but not used):

Mode d_h (default) d_v (default) s_v (default) d_h (sas) d_v (sas) s_v (sas, not used) TX 50 m 25 m 0 m 190 m 50 m 0 m TO 50 m 25 m 0 m 720 m 180 m 0 m CL 50 m 25 m −100 m 660 m 170 m −173 m AP 50 m 25 m −100 m 390 m 100 m −138 m

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• EMEP/EEA air pollutant emission inventory guidebook 2019 (Update Oct. 2020) and 2023 (Update 2025), chapters 1.A.3.b.i-iv (road transport exhaust) and 1.A.3.b.v (gasoline evaporation).
  • COPERT 5.4.52, EMISIA for the European Environment Agency.
  • US EPA AP-42, sections 1.4 (natural gas combustion), 3.3 (gasoline and diesel industrial engines) and 3.4 (large stationary diesel engines).
  • EUROCONTROL, Derivation of Smooth and Shift parameters for ALAQS-AV, EEC/SEE/2005/016.

See also: Reference data, Aircraft emissions, User Guide: define emission sources, Dispersion with AUSTAL.

docs.title: Dispersion modelling with AUSTAL
docs.text:
This page explains how to turn an OpenALAQS emission inventory into concentrations with the AUSTAL dispersion model, and how to view the results in QGIS. It is for users of the QGIS plugin who have already built an inventory (see the User Guide).

Contents: - Two ways to prepare an AUSTAL run - Before you start - Calculate Dispersion dialog - Dispersion Models tab - Site parameters - AUSTAL input files - AUSTAL output files - Results - Typical session - Common failure modes

docs.title: Two ways to prepare an AUSTAL run
docs.text:
AUSTAL is the reference dispersion model of the German TA Luft. OpenALAQS writes its input files, starts it, and reads its output. You can prepare the input files in two places:

  • Calculate Dispersion dialog (toolbar button Calculate Dispersion). The usual path. It writes the input files from an inventory file (*_out.alaqs) or from CSV files, runs AUSTAL and shows the results. See Calculate Dispersion dialog.
  • Dispersion Models tab of the Emission Inventory Analysis window (toolbar button Visualize Emission Calculation). It writes the input files while you calculate emissions, with the same method and settings as that calculation. You then run AUSTAL from the Calculate Dispersion dialog. See Dispersion Models tab.

The two paths differ in what they let you set:

Calculate Dispersion dialog Dispersion Models tab Emission method set in the inventory option, with the same choices as the Configuration tab; default bymode, no NOx correction, no source dynamics the method and settings of the Configuration tab (for example BFFM2) Pollutants any of CO2, CO, HC, NOx, SOx, PM10 in one run the one pollutant selected in the window Site parameters z0, d0, ha set in the dialog; default 0.1 / 0.6 / 10.6 m set on the tab Receptor points Receptors CSV Receptor Points of the Configuration tab Per-hour output (NOTALUFT) a check box type it into Options String Runs AUSTAL yes no: run it from the dialog with Use Existing AUSTAL Input Files

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• AUSTAL is installed and its austal.settings is replaced with the OpenALAQS copy. Without that copy, AUSTAL does not know the CO2, CO, HC and SOx substances that OpenALAQS writes. See AUSTAL installation.
  • You have an inventory file (*_out.alaqs) made with Calculate Emissions Inventory. It holds the sources, movements, meteorology and the calculation grid. See Calculate Emissions Inventory window.
  • Optional: receptor points. Without them AUSTAL produces only concentration maps; with them it also produces hourly time series at each point, which the time series plot and the compliance report need.

docs.title: Calculate Dispersion dialog
docs.text:
Click Calculate Dispersion on the OpenALAQS toolbar:

The AUSTAL Dispersion Analysis dialog has four numbered sections. Work through them in order. Each section has a status line that turns green when its inputs are complete.

docs.title: 1. AUSTAL Executable
docs.text:
Use the file picker to select austal.exe (Windows) or austal (Linux). The picker shows only files with these names. The status line then reads Executable Loaded. The path is remembered, so you do this once per computer.

The AUSTAL Help button opens a short reminder of where to download AUSTAL, which austal.settings to use and where to find the English language files, with links to the AUSTAL installation page.

docs.title: 2. Input File Strategy
docs.text:
Choose where AUSTAL's input files come from. Pick one of three options; each shows its own fields.

Option Use it when Use Existing AUSTAL Input Files You already have a folder with austal.txt, series.dmna and the emission grid files, for example from the Dispersion Models tab. Set Work Directory to that folder. Nothing is generated; AUSTAL runs in that folder. Generate AUSTAL Input Files from OpenALAQS Emission Inventory File The usual case. Set OpenALAQS Emission Inventory File to your *_out.alaqs and Output Work Directory to a folder for the run. Generate AUSTAL Input Files from CSV You have an emissions CSV and a meteorology CSV prepared outside the inventory. Set Output Directory, Emissions CSV File and Meteorology CSV File. The CSV formats are described in the austal_from_csv README.

The two Generate options share these fields:

  • Pollutants: CO2, CO, HC, NOx, SOx, PM10. Tick at least one. Only the ticked pollutants are written.
  • Quality Level (1-3): default 3. Each step up doubles the number of simulation particles in AUSTAL: less statistical noise, longer run.
  • Include Mixing Height: when ticked, AUSTAL uses the mixing height of each hour of the meteorology. When not ticked, AUSTAL applies its own mixing height.
  • Receptors CSV (optional): points where AUSTAL writes hourly time series. The format, the limit of 20 points and which points are used when the picker is empty or the file cannot be read are in Receptor points.
  • Output Mode: Per-hour series (NOTALUFT): when ticked, AUSTAL writes one concentration file per hour and, with receptors, a time series per receptor. Without it, AUSTAL writes only the mean over the run. See AUSTAL output files for which result needs what.
  • Start (incl.) / End (incl.): the part of the data to disperse. They fill in with the full time range when you select the inventory or emissions file. A period outside the data stops the generation with a message giving the available range.
  • PM10 fine fraction (0-1): default 0.9. AUSTAL treats PM10 as two size classes: fine (below 2.5 µm) and coarse (2.5 to 10 µm). This value is the fine share. 0.9 suits a typical airport mix (aircraft, ground support equipment, vehicle exhaust); the tooltip suggests 0.95 for pure aircraft exhaust, 0.70 for road traffic with tyre and brake wear, 0.40 to 0.50 for wear or dust dominated sources.
  • Roughness Length, Displacement Height, Anemometer Height: the site parameters z0, d0 and ha written to austal.txt. Defaults 0.1 m, 0 and 0. A value of 0 in Displacement Height or Anemometer Height derives it from z0 (6 × z0 and 10 m + d0), so the defaults give 0.1 / 0.6 / 10.6 m and changing z0 alone keeps the three consistent. Anemometer Height must be above Displacement Height, or the generation stops with a message.

Only the inventory option has the emission settings, since it recalculates the emissions. They are the settings of the Configuration tab of Visualize Emission Calculation, see Calculate emissions and query results. The defaults are the settings used before these fields existed:

  • Method: bymode (default) or BFFM2. BFFM2 changes the fuel flow and the emission indices of CO, HC and NOx. The other pollutants keep their per-mode emission indices, applied to the BFFM2 fuel flow, as in any BFFM2 calculation. So with BFFM2 the CO2, SOx and PM10 inputs change too.
  • Apply NOx Corrections: not ticked by default.
  • Atmosphere Aloft: standard_lapse by default. With surface_layer the profile uses the site parameters of this dialog.
  • BFFM2 Fuel-Flow Source: trajectory by default. Used only with BFFM2.
  • Source Dynamics: none by default.

Only the CSV option has the Grid Configuration box, since there is no inventory to take the grid from:

  • Grid File: an *_out.alaqs or a grid CSV; its grid fills Grid Details.
  • Grid Details: X/Y/Z Cells, X/Y/Z Resolution (m), Reference Latitude/Longitude (°) and Reference Altitude (m). You can type the grid here instead of loading a file. Cell sizes are true ground metres: the grid is built in the local UTM zone.
  • Save Grid as CSV writes the grid to a new CSV. Update File writes the edited grid back into the selected grid file.

With the inventory option the grid is always the inventory's calculation grid.

AUSTAL needs square cells. If the X and Y resolutions differ, the smaller one is used for both. AUSTAL's calculation grid is the emission grid plus two cells on every side.

docs.title: Generate AUSTAL Input Files
docs.text:
When the status line of your option is green, click Generate AUSTAL Input Files. The plugin:

  1. creates a folder AUSTAL inside the output folder you chose. If that folder is not empty, it asks before deleting its contents;
  2. with the inventory option, recalculates the emissions of all sources from the inventory with the emission settings above for the selected period;
  3. writes the AUSTAL input files into AUSTAL, with the site parameters of the dialog.

The status line then shows the path of the AUSTAL folder. Run AUSTAL becomes available. If you switch to another option, generate again before running.

docs.title: 3. Execution
docs.text:
• Erase Log File at Start of Calculation: AUSTAL starts a new austal.log instead of appending to the old one.
  • Run AUSTAL: with a Generate option it is available only after a successful generation; with Use Existing AUSTAL Input Files, as soon as the work directory is valid.

When you click Run AUSTAL, the plugin checks sections 1 and 2. If something is missing, a message names it and nothing runs. Otherwise AUSTAL runs in the AUSTAL folder (or in your work directory) and opens its own console window, where you can follow its progress. QGIS waits until AUSTAL ends. A run can take from minutes to hours, depending on the grid, the period and the quality level.

When AUSTAL ends without error, the status line turns green and a message confirms the run. When it fails, a message gives AUSTAL's exit code and the last 40 lines of austal.log (or points to the console window if there is no log).

docs.title: 4. Result Visualisation
docs.text: This section shows the results of the run. See Results.

docs.title: Dispersion Models tab
docs.text:
The Emission Inventory Analysis window (toolbar button Visualize Emission Calculation) has a Dispersion Models tab with an AUSTAL page. Use it when the AUSTAL inputs must come from the emission calculation of that window, for one pollutant at a time.

Setting Default Meaning Is Enabled not ticked Tick to write AUSTAL input files during the next calculation. Title empty Title written into austal.txt. Include Mixing Height not ticked As in the dialog: AUSTAL uses the hourly mixing height of the meteorology. Needs NOSTANDARD in the options string. Roughness Length see Site parameters z0. Displacement Height see Site parameters d0. 0 means "derive from z0". Anemometer Height see Site parameters ha. 0 means "derive from z0". Quality Level 1 1 to 10; each step up doubles the number of particles. Options String NOSTANDARD;SCINOTAT;Kmax=1 AUSTAL options, separated by semicolons. NOSTANDARD allows non-standard settings (needed for the mixing height and for Kmax); SCINOTAT writes the results in scientific notation; Kmax=1 writes only the ground layer of concentrations (Kmax=3 writes three layers). Add NOTALUFT for per-hour output.

To write the input files:

  1. Set the Configuration tab as for any emission calculation (method, period, Receptor Points if you want receptor time series). See Calculate emissions and query results.
  2. On the Dispersion Models tab, tick Is Enabled and set the values above.
  3. Select the pollutant in the window and click an output button (View Emissions Table is fastest).
  4. The plugin asks for an output folder (AUSTAL: Select Output directory). If the folder is not empty, it asks whether to delete the files in it.
  5. Open Calculate Dispersion, select Use Existing AUSTAL Input Files with that folder as Work Directory, and click Run AUSTAL.

The site parameters of this tab are also used for the surface_layer atmosphere aloft of the emission calculation, whether Is Enabled is ticked or not.

docs.title: Site parameters
docs.text:
The AUSTAL input file holds three site parameters. AUSTAL derives its wind and turbulence profiles, and so the dilution of every source, from them and the hourly wind. OpenALAQS also uses them for the surface_layer atmosphere aloft, where their effect on emissions is small: under 0.2 % in NOx on a test day.

Parameter Meaning How to set it z0, Roughness Length (m) aerodynamic roughness of the area around the sources from the land cover around the sources (step 1) d0, Displacement Height (m) height by which the profiles are shifted up over vegetation or buildings 6 × z0 (AUSTAL default) unless there is a reason to deviate ha, Anemometer Height (m) the height at which the meteo file's wind applies, for the roughness z0 from the anemometer's real height and its own surroundings (step 2); 10 m + d0 only if the anemometer stands on ground as rough as z0

docs.title: Step 1: z0 from the land cover
docs.text:
AUSTAL implements TA Luft (2021, Anhang 2). Its rule for z0: 1. For each source, take the area-weighted mean of the TA Luft z0 values of the land cover within a circle around the source. The radius is 15 × the source height, at least 150 m. 2. Average over the sources; for sources of different height, weight by the square of the height. 3. Round to the nearest TA Luft class: 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.50, 1.0, 1.5 or 2.0 m.

Outside Germany AUSTAL has no roughness register, so z0 must be entered. CORINE Land Cover (EEA, 100 m) gives the land-cover class. TA Luft values for common classes:

CORINE class z0 (m) water bodies (512) 0.01 sport and leisure (142) 0.05 airports (124), meadows and pastures (231), arable land (211) 0.10 roads and rail (122), urban green (141) 0.20 port areas (123) 0.50 discontinuous urban (112), industrial and commercial (121) 1.0 continuous urban (111) 2.0

AUSTAL takes one z0 for the whole domain. When the sources sit on very different ground, choose for the question asked and say so in the report: - an airport-only study takes the airport's value; - a study that adds city road traffic takes the value over all sources, or runs both as a sensitivity.

Example (Rotterdam The Hague, 2025 sources, CORINE 2018): - airport ground sources, emission-weighted: 0.105 m, class 0.10; - roads: 0.65 to 0.69 m, class 0.50.

docs.title: Step 2: ha for that z0
docs.text:
The meteo file's wind was measured at a real height h over the anemometer site's own roughness z0s, normally 10 m over grass at an airfield. AUSTAL instead reads the wind as if measured at height ha over ground of roughness z0. - Same roughness (z0s = z0): ha = 10 m + d0, which is AUSTAL's default. - Different roughness: ha is the equivalent height at which the profile over z0 gives the measured speed. German DWD time series (AKTerm) carry one such height per roughness class for this reason (AUSTAL manual, section 3.5.1).

Using 10 m + d0 when the site is smoother than z0 makes AUSTAL overestimate u* and the dilution, so concentrations come out low.

Order of magnitude (neutral log profiles, equal wind at 100 to 200 m; an approximation, not the DWD procedure) for a 10 m anemometer over z0s = 0.03 to 0.10 m:

z0 of the study d0 = 6 z0 ha 0.10 0.6 10 to 15 m 0.20 1.2 13 to 20 m 0.50 3.0 19 to 28 m 1.0 6.0 25 to 37 m

Where the met service supplies equivalent anemometer heights, use those. In the Netherlands, KNMI also publishes "potential wind": hourly wind at 10 m, reduced to a standard roughness of 0.03 m. With that series z0s = 0.03 m by construction.

docs.title: Step 3: keep the meteo file consistent
docs.text: The Obukhov length L in the meteorology describes stability for a roughness too. AUSTAL's own conversion from stability class to L (TA Luft, Klug/Manier classes) depends on z0. A meteo file whose L was made for another roughness, or without one, gives profiles that are inconsistent with z0. The METAR converter assigns L independently of z0, a known limitation.

docs.title: Where to set them
docs.text:
Tool Setting Default Plugin, Dispersion Models tab of Visualize Emission Calculation Roughness Length, Displacement Height, Anemometer Height 0.1 / 0.6 / 10.6 m; 0 in Displacement Height or Anemometer Height derives it from z0 Plugin, Calculate Dispersion dialog (Generate AUSTAL Input Files) Roughness Length, Displacement Height, Anemometer Height, in each Generate option 0.1 m, 0, 0, which give 0.1 / 0.6 / 10.6 m; 0 in Displacement Height or Anemometer Height derives it from z0 Standalone austal subcommand, austal_prep, Dataiku recipe --z0, --d0, --ha; z0, d0, ha in config.json and recipe_config.json 0.1 m / 6 z0 / 10 m + d0; an empty or null value is derived from z0 surface_layer without an AUSTAL module (plugin, standalone aircraft, headless runner) --z0, --d0, --ha; atmosphere_z0_m, atmosphere_d0_m, atmosphere_ha_m as the AUSTAL module

Current behaviour in the plugin. The values on the Dispersion Models tab are used for the surface_layer atmosphere aloft and for the AUSTAL input files that the tab writes when Is Enabled is ticked. The Calculate Dispersion dialog has its own fields: Generate AUSTAL Input Files writes them into austal.txt and, with the inventory option, uses them for the surface_layer atmosphere aloft.

Defaults. The plugin, the standalone and austal_prep share one default: z0 = 0.1 m, the TA Luft value for airports (class 124), the land use around most airport sources; d0 = 6 z0 and ha = 10 m + d0, AUSTAL's own defaults, consistent with each other when the anemometer stands on the airfield. d0 and ha are derived from z0 whenever they are left empty, so changing z0 alone keeps the three consistent. These defaults changed in 5.4.1, and so do the results of studies that keep them; see Upgrading from 5.4.0.

Report the three values and how they were chosen with every AUSTAL result.

docs.title: AUSTAL input files
docs.text:
Both paths write the same set of files. For the dialog's Generate options they go into AUSTAL inside the folder you chose.

File Content austal.txt Main input: title, quality level, site parameters (z0, d0, ha), hm ? when the mixing height is included, calculation grid (mesh width, origin, number of meshes), receptor points if any (positions and heights), options string, and one column per AUSTAL source whose values are marked ? (read from series.dmna). series.dmna Hourly time series: wind direction, wind speed, Obukhov length (and mixing height when included), and for each source the emission grid file index and the emission rate of each pollutant. NN/eNNNN.dmna 3D emission grids, one subfolder NN per AUSTAL source. The non-stationary sources (movements, gates, taxiways) start at 01/ with one file per hour; each stationary source group has its own folder with a single e0001.dmna for the whole run.

The options string in austal.txt, as written by the dialog, is NOSTANDARD;NOTALUFT;SCINOTAT;Kmax=1 with NOTALUFT ticked and NOSTANDARD;SCINOTAT;Kmax=1 without it. SCINOTAT writes the results in scientific notation, so small concentrations keep their digits. NOSTANDARD is always set because AUSTAL needs it to read the mixing height from series.dmna.

PM10 is written as two AUSTAL emission lines, pm-1 (fine) and pm-2 (coarse), split by the PM10 fine fraction. AUSTAL sums them in its pm result.

See the AUSTAL documentation for the meaning of every input parameter.

docs.title: AUSTAL output files
docs.text:
AUSTAL writes its results and austal.log into the folder of austal.txt:

<output folder>/AUSTAL/
├── austal.txt                 # input (generated, or yours with "Use Existing")
├── series.dmna                # input time series
├── 01/, 02/, ...              # input emission grids (eNNNN.dmna)
├── austal.log                 # run log
├── <substance>-y00a.dmna      # mean concentration grid over the run (always)
├── <substance>-y00s.dmna      # its statistical uncertainty (always)
├── <substance>-NNNa.dmna      # one grid per hour, NNN = hour index (NOTALUFT only)
└── <substance>-tmpa.dmna      # hourly time series at the receptors (receptors + NOTALUFT only)

<substance> is the AUSTAL code: co2, co, hc, nox, sox (defined in the OpenALAQS austal.settings) and pm for PM10. In y00a, 00 is the grid number and a means additional load. Concentrations are in µg/m³ (CO2 in mg/m³). By default only the ground layer is written; Kmax in the options string writes more layers.

File Written when Used by <substance>-y00a.dmna always Plot Vector Layer, averaging annual mean <substance>-y00s.dmna always not read by the plugin; statistical uncertainty of y00a <substance>-NNNa.dmna NOTALUFT Plot Vector Layer, averaging hourly or 8-hours mean <substance>-tmpa.dmna NOTALUFT and receptor points Plot Time Series, Compliance Report

"Annual mean" is the mean over the simulated period. For a run shorter than a year it is not an annual mean in the regulatory sense.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Section 4 of the Calculate Dispersion dialog, Result Visualisation, reads the AUSTAL output files and shows them in three ways.

Which folder is read. After a run, the buttons read the folder where AUSTAL ran. To view an earlier run, select Use Existing AUSTAL Input Files, tick Load Existing Results and set its Work Directory to the folder with the .dmna result files. The pollutant and averaging lists then offer what was found in that folder.

Grid Management. Tick it and set File to the inventory (*_out.alaqs) of the run. All three buttons need it: the plugin takes the period and, for the map, the grid from that file. Use the same inventory that the input files were generated from, otherwise the cells are drawn in the wrong place. The last file chosen is remembered.

Calculation Configuration. Start (incl.) and End (incl.) show the period of the inventory (read only). Averaging (hourly, 8-hours mean, daily mean, annual mean; default annual mean) and Pollutant select what Plot Vector Layer shows.

Button What you get Needs Plot Vector Layer A polygon layer on the QGIS canvas, one square per grid cell, with the concentration as attribute and a graduated colour ramp. annual mean reads y00a; hourly and 8-hours mean combine the per-hour files. daily mean is not available for the map; use the receptor results for daily values. The Grid Management file and the result file of the chosen averaging. Plot Time Series A plot of concentration against time at each receptor, with a smoothing list (Raw (hourly), 8-hour rolling mean, 24-hour rolling mean, Monthly mean), a zoom toolbar and Export CSV. *-tmpa.dmna files: a run with receptor points and NOTALUFT. Compliance Report A table per receptor and limit: value, limit, allowed exceedances and PASS/FAIL in colour, with CSV export. As for Plot Time Series.

The line below the buttons lists the substances with receptor results, or says what is missing. The tooltip of a disabled button gives the steps to enable it: add receptor points, tick NOTALUFT, generate the input files again and run AUSTAL again.

docs.title: The concentration map
docs.text: The layer is drawn in the UTM zone of the study, so each cell is a true square of the mesh width. It is a normal QGIS vector layer: you can change its symbology, click cells to read values, open its attribute table or save it as a GeoPackage. A new plot of the same name replaces the old layer.

docs.title: The compliance report
docs.text:
The report compares each receptor with the limit values of Directive (EU) 2024/2881 (Annex I, Section 1) that apply from 1 January 2030, and NOx with the critical level for the protection of vegetation. The header line states the directive and how many receptors and substances were evaluated.

Substance Annual mean (µg/m³) Daily mean (µg/m³, exceedances allowed per year) Hourly mean (µg/m³, exceedances allowed per year) PM10 20 45 (18) PM2.5 10 25 (18) NO2 20 200 (3) NOx: critical level for the protection of vegetation, not a limit value (the report labels the row "NOx") 30 SO2 20 50 (treated as no exceedance allowed, pending verification of the count)

Notes: - The annual mean is the mean of the hours of the run, and the exceedances are counted over the run. For a run shorter than a year, read the result as an indication only. - CO, HC and CO2 have no comparable EU ambient limit and are not reported. - A run from the dialog produces only the pollutants of its check boxes, so the report shows rows for PM10 and NOx only. No check box writes PM2.5, NO2 or SO2.

docs.title: Typical session
docs.text:
1. Open Calculate Dispersion.
  2. Section 1: select the AUSTAL executable (once per computer).
  3. Section 2: select Generate AUSTAL Input Files from OpenALAQS Emission Inventory File. Set the inventory file, the Output Work Directory, the pollutants, the quality level and the period.
  4. For receptor results: give a Receptors CSV and tick NOTALUFT.
  5. Click Generate AUSTAL Input Files and wait for the status line to show the AUSTAL folder.
  6. Section 3: click Run AUSTAL and wait for the green status line.
  7. Section 4: tick Grid Management and set File to the same inventory.
  8. Click Plot Vector Layer for the concentration map, or, with receptors and NOTALUFT, Plot Time Series or Compliance Report.

docs.title: Common failure modes
docs.text:
• "No Executable Loaded" after picking a file. The picker accepts only files named austal.exe or austal. Rename a file such as austal_3.exe.
  • The run fails, or the results of some substances are missing. Check that the AUSTAL folder has the OpenALAQS austal.settings. It defines the CO2, CO, HC and SOx substances that are not among AUSTAL's standard ones. See Configuration files.
  • "AUSTAL input files could not be created: the selected time period". Start or End is outside the inventory or emissions file. The message gives the available range.
  • A result button says "No emission calculation loaded". Set Grid Management > File to the inventory.
  • Plot Vector Layer stays disabled. No run has finished in this session and no results folder is loaded under Load Existing Results.
  • Plot Time Series and Compliance Report stay disabled. There are no *-tmpa.dmna files: the run had no receptor points or no NOTALUFT. Set both, generate again and run again.
  • Plot Vector Layer says it "can't aggregate" to the period. The averaging needs files that the run did not write (hourly or 8-hours mean without NOTALUFT), or it is daily mean. Use annual mean for the map and the receptor results for hourly and daily values.
  • Cells appear in the wrong place. The Grid Management file is not the inventory the inputs were generated from. Select the same inventory.
  • A long run seems stuck. Watch AUSTAL's console window, or check that austal.log in the run folder is still growing.

docs.title: In the code
docs.text: For maintainers: the dialog is open_alaqs/gui/DispersionAnalysis.py with open_alaqs/ui/ui_run_austal.ui; the input files are written by open_alaqs/core/modules/AUSTALOutputModule.py (CSV option: open_alaqs/core/tools/austal_csv_generation.py); the results by ConcentrationsQGISVectorLayerOutputModule.py, TimeSeriesDispersionOutputModule.py and ComplianceReportOutputModule.py in open_alaqs/core/modules/. The site-parameter default is site_parameters() in open_alaqs/core/tools/surface_layer_atmosphere.py.

docs.title: Input file formats
docs.text:
This page describes the CSV files you give OpenALAQS: aircraft movements, meteorology, ADS-B tracks, engine test events and receptor points. It is for users who prepare these files for a study. Each section gives the delimiter, the columns and an example taken from the training files in example/training/.

  • Movements
  • Meteorology
  • ADS-B tracks
  • Engine test events
  • Receptor points

docs.title: Movements
docs.text:
One row per aircraft movement (arrival or departure, fixed-wing or helicopter). You select the file in Movements Table of the Calculate Emissions Inventory window (see Calculate Emissions Inventory window).

Delimiter: semicolon (;) only. A comma-separated file is not read.

Header: the first row names the columns. Write the names exactly as in the table below. Every column must be in the header, even when its values are empty; only gate_emissions_code may be left out. The plugin then maps the columns by name. A trailing domestic column (old files) is ignored.

If any name is missing, misspelt or unknown, the plugin ignores the whole header and reads every column by position. A file without a header line (its first row starts with a date) is also read by position, and its first row is kept as a movement. A row of 20 fields is read in the order of the table below. Any other row is read in the old order of 19 columns: the table below without gate_emissions_code, which then takes its default. If the header ends with domestic (old files), every row is read in the old order of 19 columns, followed by gate_emissions_code when the row has it; the domestic value is ignored. The log shows a warning that names the unknown and missing header names. Keep runway_time as the first column: the file check reads the date range from it.

Dates: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS. When you select the file, every row is checked. A single row whose first field is not such a date, or that has fewer than 10 fields, refuses the whole file: the status line reads "Problem with movement file. See log file", and the log names the row.

Column Unit Required Meaning Default when empty runway_time date and time yes Time on the runway: for an arrival the touchdown (A-CDM ALDT), for a departure the start of the take-off roll. An A-CDM take-off time (ATOT) is wheels-off: take the take-off roll off it first. block_time date and time yes Time at the gate: in-block for an arrival, off-block for a departure. The taxi time is the difference between the two times; for an arrival the landing roll of its profile is taken out of it. aircraft yes ICAO aircraft type designator. For a helicopter, the ICAO code or a variant label of the helicopter catalog (see Helicopters). gate yes Name of the gate (as in the Gates layer). departure_arrival yes A = arrival, D = departure. runway yes Runway end used (as in the Runways layer, for example 24). engine_name no Engine identifier from the engine table. the aircraft's default engine profile_id no Flight profile. An ANP profile, or the flight_id of an imported ADS-B flight (see ADS-B tracks). the aircraft's default profile track_id no Name of a track of the Tracks layer (shapes_tracks) with the movement's runway and direction: the plugin lays the flight profile along it, which changes the trajectory and the emissions. The standalone pipeline does not follow tracks. taxi_route yes Name of the taxi route, as built in the Taxiway Routes Editor (gate/runway/A or D/instance, for example G4/24/A/1). tow_ratio fraction (at most 1.0) no Take-off weight divided by the maximum take-off weight. Used only by the bymode NOx correction, on take-off and climb-out. 0, a negative value or NaN is replaced by 1, with a warning in the log. 1.0 apu_code no APU use: -1 or 0 no APU; 1 APU at the stand only; 2 APU during the whole taxi. 0 gate_emissions_code no 0 leaves out the gate emissions (GSE, GPU and main engine start) of this movement; 1 includes them. 1 taxi_engine_count engines no Engines running during taxi (single-engine taxi). Never more than the aircraft's engines. 2 set_time_of_main_engine_start_after_block_off_in_s s no Departure: time after off-block during which the aircraft taxis on taxi_engine_count engines. Used before the next column when both are set. set_time_of_main_engine_start_before_takeoff_in_s s no Departure: time before take-off at which the other engines are started. set_time_of_main_engine_off_after_runway_exit_in_s s no Arrival: time after the runway exit during which all engines run before the others are shut down. engine_thrust_level_for_taxiing fraction no Taxi thrust (0.07 = 7 %, the ICAO value). Used by BFFM2 only; bymode uses the taxi (TX) mode values. A value below 0 or above 1.05 (for example 7 for 7 %) is rejected with an error in the log, and the taxi then uses the TX mode values. 0.07 taxi_fuel_ratio ratio no Single-engine taxi fuel flow divided by the idle fuel flow. Multiplies the emissions of the taxi segments in single-engine taxi (and of the single-engine part of a departure's queue) only; taxi on all engines is not affected, so it has no effect without a main engine start or off time. Plugin and standalone alike. 1.0 number_of_stop_and_gos count no Stop-and-go events during taxi. Each adds a short burst at the taxi emission index to the queuing segment. 0

How the taxi columns are used is described in Aircraft emissions: taxiing and APU, GSE and engine start.

Example (header and first two rows of example/training/training_movements.csv):

runway_time;block_time;aircraft;gate;departure_arrival;runway;engine_name;profile_id;track_id;taxi_route;tow_ratio;apu_code;gate_emissions_code;taxi_engine_count;set_time_of_main_engine_start_after_block_off_in_s;set_time_of_main_engine_start_before_takeoff_in_s;set_time_of_main_engine_off_after_runway_exit_in_s;engine_thrust_level_for_taxiing;taxi_fuel_ratio;number_of_stop_and_gos
2025-12-01 06:05:00;2025-12-01 06:10:00;A20N;G4;A;24;01P20CM128;JET-SMALL-A-1;;G4/24/A/1;;0;0;2;;;;0.07;1;0
