docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
OpenALAQS is a EUROCONTROL open-source tool that models emissions from aircraft operations and other airport sources. It calculates emission inventories, shows them on the map, and prepares and runs dispersion calculations with AUSTAL.

It is a plugin for the open-source geographic information system QGIS. You draw the airport elements (runways, taxiways, gates, buildings, ...) as QGIS layers and see the spatial distribution of emissions and concentrations on the map.

To install the plugin, see Installation. To open a study made with an earlier version, see Upgrading.

docs.title: Workflow at a glance
docs.text:
A study goes through these steps, in the order of the toolbar buttons:

  1. Create the study: airport, road traffic settings.
  2. Draw the emission sources: gates, runways, taxiways, stationary sources, and their activity profiles.
  3. Define the taxi routes and generate the emission inventory from the movements, meteo and (optionally) ADS-B files.
  4. Calculate the emissions and look at the results: tables, time series, maps.
  5. Optionally, run AUSTAL for concentrations.

The tutorial goes through all steps with the training data.

docs.title: The OpenALAQS Toolbar
docs.text:
The toolbar has these buttons (the names are the button tooltips):

  • About Open ALAQS: the plugin version and general information.
  • Create an Open ALAQS project: create a new study.
  • Load an Open ALAQS project: open an existing study.
  • Close all Open ALAQS projects: close the current study.
  • Airport Study Setup: general information about the study (window ALAQS Project Properties).
  • Import OSM data: download and import data from OpenStreetMap (OSM).
  • Edit profiles: create activity profiles (hourly, daily, monthly; window Open ALAQS - Activity Profiles).
  • Define taxi routes: build taxi routes from the gates, runways and taxiways (window Taxiway Routes Editor).
  • Calculate Emissions Inventory: write the inventory file with all study data (window Generate Emission Inventory).
  • Visualize Emission Calculation: calculate the emissions, show and export the results (window Emission Inventory Analysis).
  • Calculate Dispersion: prepare and run AUSTAL (window AUSTAL Dispersion Analysis).
  • Review Open ALAQS logs: open the log file. Besides errors, it lists warnings about the input, for example an ADS-B fuel flow far above the take-off fuel flow or below idle, an arrival that leaves the runway above 50 kt, or duplicate gate names after an OSM import.
  • Open ALAQS documentation: open this documentation, for the installed plugin version, in the web browser.

The order of the buttons follows the steps of a study.

docs.title: Setup a new study
docs.text:
Click Create an Open ALAQS project. In the window Create an Open ALAQS project file, choose a File name for the new study (.alaqs).

The ALAQS Project Properties window then opens. On the Airport tab, enter a project name and at least the ICAO code of the airport. The other fields (airport name, country, latitude, longitude, ...) are filled from the plugin's airport list; you can edit them.

The Vertical Limit field of the Airport tab is greyed out because it is not used: the LTO ceiling of each hour is the mixing height of the meteo file, or 914.4 m when there is none (see LTO ceiling).

The Roadways tab holds the settings for road traffic emissions with COPERT: the average fleet year (1990 to 2030 in steps of 5) and the country for country-specific emission factors (or EU27). The fleet year stands for the average age of the fleet, and so for its mix of Euro 1 to Euro 6 vehicle standards.

Airport Study Setup opens the same window later.

docs.title: Open an existing study
docs.text: Click Load an Open ALAQS project and select the study file (.alaqs) in the window Open an ALAQS database file.

docs.title: Import OpenStreetMap data
docs.text:
Import OSM data creates sources from OpenStreetMap data (runways, taxiways, gates, buildings, roads, ...).

There is no search box: the plugin finds the aerodrome on Nominatim from the study's ICAO code, then downloads its data from OpenStreetMap. In the dialog:

  • Selective import: tick it, then tick the layer types to download. When it is not ticked, every layer type is downloaded.
  • Also import the data into ALAQS database: tick it to create the features in the study's layers (Runways, Taxiways, Gates, ...). Without it, the data only appear as the layers OSM Points, OSM Lines and OSM Polygons in a group OpenStreetMap Layers, for reference.

The study setup must have the airport latitude and longitude. Without them the import does nothing, with no message. The import needs the QuickOSM QGIS plugin; without it, the dialog says so and the import is disabled. The image below shows what can be collected.

The log reports the number of buildings imported and where their heights come from: the OSM height value when the feature has one, else 0 m. With the bundled OSM reader configuration the height is not available, so imported buildings get 0 m; enter the heights by hand.

Gate names come from the OSM ref tag of the aprons. When an imported name is already in the Gates layer, or occurs twice in the import, the log warns with the names, for example OSM import: gate name(s) already in layer "Gates": G7; check and rename before calculating. The features are imported as they are. Rename or delete the duplicates before calculating (see Gates).

docs.title: Add, edit and delete features
docs.text:
Draw new features with the QGIS Digitizing toolbar.

The QGIS User Manual explains this toolbar.

To create a source, select its layer (for example Taxiways or Runways), click Toggle Editing, then Add Feature, and draw. Right-click to finish and fill in the form.

To change a geometry, use the Vertex Tool in editing mode. To delete features, select them (Select Features by area or single click, or in the attribute table) and click Delete Selected.

docs.title: Visualize and Edit Attribute Values
docs.text:
You can change the attributes of a feature after it is created, with the Attributes toolbar.

Open Attribute Table is on the Attributes toolbar and in the right-click menu of the layer in the Layers panel.

The attribute table uses the field names of the forms and of this guide (for example Touchdown Offset, Runway 1 [m] or Vehicles per Year). In Study is the last column, shown as true / false. On parkings, roadways, point sources and area sources it is also a check box in the form, right under the name: unticked sources are left out of the emission calculation. It is hidden on the other layers, which do not use it. New features start with the form defaults: heights and offsets 0, profiles default, Gate Type PIER and In Study ticked.

docs.title: Aircraft related Sources
docs.text: Aircraft emissions need three layers: runways, taxiways and gates, each with its required attributes. Tracks (custom aircraft trajectories) can be drawn too, but this function is not yet fully implemented.

docs.title: Gates
docs.text:
A gate is where aircraft park for boarding, loading and services (refuelling, catering, maintenance).

In OpenALAQS a gate is a polygon and can hold several aircraft stands. The more stands one gate holds, the less preparation is needed (for example fewer taxi routes). A gate that is too large no longer places the emissions well.

Gate emissions are the sum of four sources: ground support equipment (GSE), ground power unit (GPU), auxiliary power unit (APU) and main engine start (MES).

A gate needs: + Gate Name + Gate Type (PIER, REMOTE or CARGO). The type selects the GSE and GPU emission factors, together with the aircraft category and the operation (arrival or departure). + Height [m] (not yet fully implemented)

Gate names should be unique: movements refer to gates by name, and with two gates of the same name the calculation uses only one of them. When another gate already has the name, the form colours the Gate Name box yellow and its tooltip says so; the gate can still be saved.

How the gate, APU and engine start emissions are calculated is described in APU, GSE and engine start.

docs.title: Runways
docs.text:
A runway is a line. It defines the vertical plane of approach, landing, take-off and climb-out. Each end of the runway is a runway direction.

A runway has: + Runway Name: built from the runway ends chosen in the form (Runway 1 and the opposite Runway 2, for example 06/24). + Touchdown Offset, Runway 1 [m]: distance from the Runway 1 end (its landing threshold) to the touchdown of arrivals landing on Runway 1. Empty or 0: each arrival profile's own distance, where the profile descends through 50 ft (15.24 m, the ILS reference datum height), about 290 m past the threshold on a 3° approach. + Touchdown Offset, Runway 2 [m]: the same for Runway 2, independently of Runway 1. Empty or 0: each arrival profile's own distance.

Both offsets are whole metres.

Draw the runway along the full pavement, from one end to the other (the drawing direction does not matter). The touchdown offset is measured from the drawn end: where the landing threshold is displaced, enter the displacement plus about 290 m; otherwise leave it empty (the profile's own 50 ft crossing, about 290 m). A profile that never descends through 50 ft touches down at the drawn end. Departures line up where their taxi route last meets the runway (see below), not at the drawn end.

Each offset is measured from its own landing threshold, along the landing direction, and applies to that direction only: for the same touchdown on both ends, enter the value in both fields.

Placement of the flight profiles on the runway. The taxi route does not move the flight profile; it is checked against it. + Arrivals (ANP profiles) touch down at the landing threshold plus the Touchdown Offset. The aircraft leaves the runway at the first point past the touchdown where its taxi route meets the runway at 50 kt or less (ICAO Doc 9157 Part 2: rapid-exit reference speed); if no crossing is that slow, at the first one past the touchdown. When that exit comes before the end of the profile's rollout, the rollout ends there. When it comes after, the aircraft rolls on along the runway to the exit; that stretch is taxiing (from the rollout-end speed down to at most 18 kt). + Departures (ANP profiles) start their take-off roll where the taxi route last meets the runway (the line-up point); a route that runs along the runway (backtracking) lines up where it leaves it. + ADS-B profiles keep their own positions. + Taxi routes are read in the direction of travel, whichever way round their taxiways are listed (stand to runway or runway to stand); the taxiways must still be listed in sequence: from the stand for a departure, to the stand for an arrival.

Nothing blocks the calculation. An exit above 50 kt, or a route that meets the runway only before the touchdown, is reported in the log. The QGIS-free tool also writes a check report (runway_checks.csv), one line per route and profile, with what to change.

Runways are named after their compass heading, rounded to the nearest 10 degrees. Since a runway can be used in both directions, its two ends have numbers that differ by 18 (180 degrees). Parallel runways add L (Left), C (Center) or R (Right).

Runway emissions follow the flight profiles of the Aircraft Noise and Performance (ANP) database, see Flight profiles.

docs.title: Taxiways
docs.text:
A taxiway connects the runways with the gates and other parts of the airport. A taxiway needs: + Taxiway Name + Speed [km/h]

The length comes from the drawn geometry, and the time on the taxiway from its length and speed. Taxi speeds depend on the conditions, the traffic and the position on the route; typical values lie between 10 and 40 km/h (about 5 to 25 kt).

Taxiways are not taxi routes. A taxi route is the path an aircraft follows for one gate, runway and operation (arrival or departure); it is a series of taxiways. See Taxi routes.

docs.title: Tracks
docs.text:
A track is a custom aircraft trajectory. A track needs: + Track Name + Runway Direction (from the runways of the study) + Operation Type (Arrival or Departure)

Tracks are not yet used by the calculation. Departure and approach trajectories come from the ANP profiles (column profile_id of the movements file). To use observed trajectories instead, give an ADS-B file when you generate the inventory and set the movement's profile_id to the ADS-B flight_id, see ADS-B tracks and ADS-B in the emission calculation.

docs.title: Helicopters (FOCA 2015)
docs.text:
Helicopter movements are in the same movements file as aircraft. Nothing marks a row as a helicopter: when the aircraft code is in the helicopter catalog, the movement is calculated as a helicopter, with the FOCA 2015 method and helicopter trajectories, whatever the Method chosen. The aircraft column takes an ICAO code (the catalog's default variant is used) or a variant label of the catalog.

No APU, GSE, GPU or main engine start emissions are calculated for helicopters, whatever apu_code and gate_emissions_code say; the gate is only the helipad. The method, the helicopter categories, the catalog and how to add a type are described in Helicopters.

docs.title: Stationary Sources
docs.text: Besides aircraft, a study can hold point sources, roadways, parking lots, area sources and buildings, each with its required attributes.

docs.title: Parking Lots
docs.text:
Parking emissions are calculated with the COPERT method, see Road traffic and parkings.

A parking lot needs: + Parking Name + Parameters + Vehicles per Year: total number of vehicles per year + Height [m]: height at which emissions are released (not yet fully implemented) + Speed [km/h]: average speed in the parking + Travel Distance [m]: average distance driven in the parking + Idle Time [min]: average idling time between entry and exit + Profiles: Hourly Profile, Daily Profile and Monthly Profile (see Activity Profiles) + Fleet mix + PC (Petrol) [%], PC (Diesel) [%]: passenger cars + LCV (Petrol) [%], LCV (Diesel) [%]: light commercial vehicles + HDT (Petrol) [%], HDT (Diesel) [%]: heavy duty trucks + Motorcycle [%] + Bus [%]

Make sure the fleet mix adds up to 100 % (Fleet Mix tab). Then click Recalculate on the Emissions tab: it fills in the emission factors (CO [g/vehicle], HC [g/vehicle], NOx [g/vehicle], SOx [g/vehicle], PM10 [g/vehicle], P1 [g/vehicle], P2 [g/vehicle]) and Method from COPERT, using the parameters above and the fleet year and country of the study setup. These fields cannot be typed.

docs.title: Roadways
docs.text:
Roadway emissions (airside or landside) use the same method as parking lots.

A roadway needs: + Roadway Name + Parameters + Vehicles per Year: number of vehicles per year on the roadway + Height [m]: height at which emissions are released (not yet fully implemented) + Speed [km/h]: vehicle speed on the roadway + Scenario: greyed out (Not Applicable); it has no effect. + Profiles: Hourly Profile, Daily Profile and Monthly Profile + Fleet mix: as for parking lots

As for parking lots, Recalculate fills in the emission factors (CO [g/km], HC [g/km], NOx [g/km], SOx [g/km], PM10 [g/km], P1 [g/km], P2 [g/km]).

docs.title: Point sources
docs.text:
Point sources are stationary emitters at the airport: power and heating plants, incinerators, training fires, fuel tanks, stationary combustion engines.

A point source needs: + Source Name + Parameters + Category: Other, Incinerator, Power/Heat Plant, Fuel Tank, Solvent Degreaser, Surface Coating or Stationary IC Engine. + Type: the type within the category, for example natural gas, light or heavy fuel oil, JP-4, JP-5, JET A, automobile gasoline, aviation gasoline. The full list is in default_stationary_ef. For a Stationary IC Engine, pick the type that matches the engine's rated power and combustion chamber. + Height [m]: height at which emissions are released (not yet fully implemented). + Activity per Year: how much the source runs in one year: throughput, fuel used or hours run. + Activity Unit: the unit of Activity per Year. It is filled in from the selected type when the Type changes, and you can change it (the emission factors must then be per that unit). Examples: 1000_m3 (natural gas), 1000_L (liquid fuel), hr (engine hours), 1000_kg (waste, coating). + Substance, Temperature [°C], Diameter [m], Gas Velocity [m/s]: the state of the release and the stack, filled in from the type. They are stored with the source; neither the emission calculation nor the AUSTAL input uses them. + Profiles: one Hourly Profile, one Daily Profile and one Monthly Profile, which spread the Activity per Year over the year. The type list suggests profile names (for example business_hours for stationary engines, heating_season for heating plants); see the example profiles for whether your study has them. Until a suggested profile exists, the source uses the uniform default profile.

The emission factors (CO [kg/unit], HC [kg/unit], NOx [kg/unit], SOx [kg/unit], PM10 [kg/unit], P1 [kg/unit], P2 [kg/unit]) come from the selected type and are in kilograms per Activity Unit. What to enter, for example:

Source Activity Activity per Year Activity Unit Heating plant on natural gas 850 000 m³ gas per year 850 1000_m3 Diesel backup generator 400 operating hours per year 400 hr Incinerator 3 200 tonnes of waste per year 3200 1000_kg Fuel storage tank 1 800 000 L throughput per year 1800 1000_L

The calculation is described in Point and area sources.

docs.title: Area sources
docs.text:
The area source layer holds sources that the other layers do not cover, when you have their emission factors.

An area source needs: + Source Name + Parameters: + Units per Year: number of operating hours (units) per year + Height [m]: height at which emissions are released (not yet fully implemented) + Heat Flux [MW]: read-only, 0 for new area sources (not yet fully implemented) + Emissions: CO [kg/unit], HC [kg/unit], NOx [kg/unit], SOx [kg/unit], PM10 [kg/unit], P1 [kg/unit], P2 [kg/unit] + Profiles: Hourly Profile, Daily Profile and Monthly Profile (default or your own)

The yearly emission is the emission factor times Units per Year, spread over the year by the profiles (see Point and area sources).

P1 and P2 are two extra pollutants you can define. For aircraft, P1 and P2 stand for PM1.0 and PM2.5 and are currently equal to PM10 (see PM10 output columns).

The form also has an Engine Test Site check box, see the next section.

docs.title: Engine test sites
docs.text:
An engine test site (run-up pad) is an area source whose emissions come from a list of engine test events, not from emission factors and profiles. Each event gives a start and end time, the aircraft type and engine, and the running time in each engine mode.

Setup:

  1. Draw an area source covering the run-up pad. Fill in the name and height as for an area source.
  2. In the source's form, tick Engine Test Site. Units per Year and the Emissions and Profiles tabs gray out: they are not used for test sites. Only Source Name and Height [m] are required.
  3. Prepare a CSV of events, one row per engine run, see Engine test events. One file can hold the events of several test sites.
  4. Load the events, in one of two ways:
  5. From the source form: click Load engine test events CSV... (enabled only when Engine Test Site is ticked). Select the file, review the summary, pick the insert mode (Append or Replace), tick "Tolerate warnings" if needed, and click Apply. Only the rows for this source are loaded; the summary counts the others ("Rows for other sources: n (skipped; not for this source)").
  6. From a terminal, for scripting or several sites at once: run python scripts/import_engine_test_events.py study.alaqs events.csv without --apply first to check the file, then with --apply. See scripts/README.md.
  7. Save the form (OK). Then generate the emission inventory again. Test site emissions appear with the other sources (as EngineTestSource).

A study made before engine test sites existed needs the migration script first, otherwise the check box has nowhere to save; see Upgrading from 5.3.x. Close and reopen the study after the migration.

By default each event uses the ICAO emission indices of each engine mode, with no ambient correction; other thrust modes cannot be set from the CSV. The calculation is described in Engine test sites.

docs.title: Buildings
docs.text:
Buildings are not emission sources, but they affect the wind and turbulence and so the dispersion. They are in the layer list for future use (not yet fully implemented).

A building needs: + Building Name + Height [m]: height of the building above ground (not yet fully implemented)

docs.title: Activity Profiles
docs.text:
Activity profiles describe how a source's activity varies by hour of the day, day of the week and month. Edit profiles opens the window Open ALAQS - Activity Profiles, where you review, edit and create profiles.

Profiles are relative shapes. Each value is a non-negative number; only the ratios between the values of a profile matter, and values above 1 are allowed. The default profiles are all 1 (uniform). Whatever the shapes, the source's annual total stays the same: the profiles only spread it over the year.

So a 0 in a profile (for example a night curfew) moves that period's emissions to the other periods; it does not lower the annual total. To lower the total, lower Activity per Year or Units per Year. A profile that is 0 everywhere gives no emissions at all. The calculation is described in Point and area sources.

Example profiles. The type list of point sources suggests the names heating_season, cooling_season and business_hours. A new study does not have them: create them with Edit profiles. A study updated with the migration script (Upgrading from 5.3.x) already has them, with the values below (1.0 where nothing is listed). They are a starting point for a temperate European airport, not reference data; adapt them to the site.

heating_season: month profile, winter-weighted (peaks in January, February and December):

Jan=2.0, Feb=1.8, Mar=1.4, Apr=0.7, May=0.3, Jun=0.1,
Jul=0.05, Aug=0.05, Sep=0.3, Oct=0.8, Nov=1.5, Dec=1.9

cooling_season: month profile, summer-weighted (peaks in July and August), with a daytime hour profile:

Jan=0.2, Feb=0.2, Mar=0.3, Apr=0.5, May=0.9, Jun=1.4,
Jul=1.8, Aug=1.8, Sep=1.2, Oct=0.6, Nov=0.3, Dec=0.2

h01=0.4, h02-h05=0.3, h06=0.4, h07=0.6, h08=0.8, h09=1.0, h10=1.2, h11=1.4, h12=1.6,
h13=1.8, h14-h16=2.0, h17=1.8, h18=1.5, h19=1.2, h20=1.0, h21=0.8, h22=0.6, h23=0.5, h24=0.4

business_hours: one hour profile and one day profile with the same name:

  • Hour profile: h01 to h06 = 0.2, h07 = 0.5, h08 to h19 = 1.5, h20 = 1.0, h21 = 0.5, h22 = 0.3, h23 to h24 = 0.2.
  • Day profile: 1.2 for Monday to Friday, 0.4 for Saturday and Sunday.

Example combinations:

Source type Month profile Day profile Hour profile Resulting timing Heating plant heating_season default default Mostly in winter; uniform within each day. Stationary IC engine default business_hours business_hours Year-round, mostly on weekdays from h08 to h19 (nights and weekends keep a small share). Cooling tower cooling_season default business_hours Summer daytime, every day.

docs.title: Generate Emissions Inventory
docs.text: This section covers the steps that prepare the emission inventory.

docs.title: Taxi routes
docs.text:
A taxi route is the path of an aircraft between the runway and the gate (see Taxiways). Define the routes in the Taxiway Routes Editor (button Define taxi routes).

The editor has two tabs. In Create new route, select the gate, the runway and the operation (arrival or departure) to create the route. Several routes can exist for the same gate, runway and operation, with different instance numbers. In Edit route, pick the route in Route ID, then list its taxiways, in order, in the Taxiways tab and the aircraft groups that may use it in the Aircraft Groups tab, and click Save Route. The route name (for example G4/24/A/1) is what the movements file refers to. The tutorial shows an example.

docs.title: Calculate Emissions Inventory window
docs.text:
Before calculating emissions, generate the inventory file. It holds all elements of the study (sources, routes, profiles) and the reference data (emission factors, profiles).

Calculate Emissions Inventory opens the window Generate Emission Inventory: + Emission Inventory Output: + Directory: the folder of the output file + File Name: the name of the output file, without extension: the plugin adds _out.alaqs (training gives training_out.alaqs) + ADS-B Data (Optional): + ADS-B Table: a file of observed flight tracks (see ADS-B tracks). It is checked when you select it; the line below the field says whether it is valid, how many flights it holds, and any warnings. A movement uses an ADS-B track when its profile_id is the track's flight_id. + Movement Data: + Movements Table: the movements file, semicolon-separated (see Movements). The file is checked when you select it; the summary shows the number of movements and their period. + Filter Start Date, Filter End Date: limit the movements to a period. They are filled from the movements file. + Meteorological Data: + Meteorological Table: the hourly meteo file: temperature, pressure, humidity, wind, stability and mixing height, from local or national providers (METAR, SYNOP) or reanalysis data. They are used by BFFM2, by the NOx correction, for the mixing height (the LTO ceiling of each hour) and for dispersion. The file is optional; columns and what happens without it: Meteorology. To convert METAR reports, use scripts/metar_to_alaqs_meteo.py. + Modelled Domain: + X Resolution: cell size and number of cells along X; default 250 m and 50 cells. + Y Resolution: the same along Y; default 250 m and 50 cells. + Z Resolution: the same in height; default 50 m and 20 cells.

Click Create Inventory to write the inventory file (<File Name>_out.alaqs in the chosen folder); Close closes the window.

docs.title: Calculate emissions and query results
docs.text:
Visualize Emission Calculation opens the window where the emissions are calculated and shown. You can browse all source types and names. Aircraft emissions (gates, taxiways and runways) are grouped under MovementSource.

The settings panel at the bottom left holds the calculation settings, the output formats and the dispersion settings.

On the Configuration tab: + Start (incl.) / End (incl.): the calculation period (optional). + Method: bymode or BFFM2. + bymode uses the ICAO emission indices of each engine mode (take-off, climb-out, approach, taxi) with the time in each mode. Simple and fast. + BFFM2 (Boeing Fuel Flow Method 2) derives the emission indices from the fuel flow of each profile segment and corrects them for the ambient conditions. It applies to CO, HC and NOx only. It usually gives less NOx than bymode. See Methods and BFFM2.

BFFM2 is offered only while the selected pollutant is CO, HC or NOx. Selecting another pollutant shows Method as bymode; selecting CO, HC or NOx again brings back BFFM2 if you had chosen it. + Apply NOx Corrections: corrects the bymode NOx of take-off and climb-out for ambient temperature, humidity and aircraft weight (tow_ratio of the movements). No effect with BFFM2, which corrects for the ambient conditions itself. See NOx ambient correction. + BFFM2 Fuel-Flow Source (BFFM2 only): trajectory (default) takes the fuel flow from each segment's power setting, or from the ADS-B track when it has one; mode_anchor takes the ICAO fuel flow of the segment's engine mode and ignores ADS-B fuel flows. The emission indices are corrected for the ambient conditions with both. Taxi uses the fuel flow at the taxi thrust with both. See Fuel-flow sources. + Atmosphere Aloft: the temperature, pressure and humidity used at each flight segment's height, from the hourly meteo. + standard_lapse (default): the ground values carried up with the ISA lapse rate. + surface_layer: the AUSTAL boundary-layer temperature profile, from the hour's wind and stability and the site parameters of the Dispersion Models tab. It is not more accurate than standard_lapse. + ground_held: the hourly ground values at every height.

See Ambient conditions aloft. + Source Dynamics: none (default), default or smooth & shift. The last two spread each trajectory segment into a volume before it enters the emission grid, to account for engine exhaust momentum, plume rise and near-field mixing. See Source dynamics. + Time Interval: the time step of the calculation (default 1 hour). + Vertical Limit: greyed out, because it does not change the result. The LTO ceiling of each hour is the mixing height of the meteo file, or 914.4 m when there is none (see LTO ceiling). + Receptor Points: a file of receptor points for the AUSTAL module of the Dispersion Models tab (optional, see Receptor points).

Changing any setting discards the previous calculation. It is calculated again when you next ask for an output (View Emissions Table, Plot Time Series, Plot Vector Layer).

On the Output Formats tab: + Emissions table: how the table is aggregated (by aggregation, by source or by grid cell) + Time Series: x-axis title, marker and receptor points + Vector Layer: settings for the map of results on the grid

The Dispersion Models tab holds the AUSTAL settings, see Dispersion.

There are three ways to see the emissions: + as a table (View Emissions Table) + as a time series (Plot Time Series) + on the grid (Plot Vector Layer)

docs.title: PM10 output columns
docs.text:
For aircraft movements, the emission output has these particulate matter columns:

Column Contents pm10_kg Total PM10: combustion PM10, plus brake wear for arrivals pm10_nonvol_kg Non-volatile PM (nvPM mass) pm10_sul_kg Sulphate volatile PM pm10_organic_kg Organic volatile PM p1_kg PM1.0 placeholder; currently equal to pm10_kg p2_kg PM2.5 placeholder; currently equal to pm10_kg

For departures, pm10_kg is the sum of the three sub-components. For arrivals it also holds the brake wear, which shows as a surplus over that sum on the first taxi segment. How each column is calculated is described in Particulate matter.

docs.title: Dispersion
docs.text: OpenALAQS prepares the input files of the AUSTAL dispersion model from the emission inventory, runs AUSTAL and shows the concentrations. The AUSTAL settings of the Visualize Emission Calculation window are on the Dispersion Models tab, including the site parameters roughness length, displacement height and anemometer height (how to choose them). The Calculate Dispersion button opens the Calculate Dispersion dialog, which generates the AUSTAL input files and runs AUSTAL. The concentration maps, time series at receptors and the compliance report are described in Results. AUSTAL itself is installed separately, see AUSTAL installation.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Input file formats: movements, meteo, ADS-B, engine test events and receptor files.
  • Tutorial with the Rotterdam training data: a full study, step by step.
  • Dispersion with AUSTAL: concentrations from the inventory.
  • Upgrading: opening a study made with an earlier version.

docs.title: Running Open-ALAQS without the QGIS window
docs.text:
Which tool to use when you want to work on a study from a terminal instead of the QGIS window. It is for users who run batch jobs, build input files or upgrade studies outside QGIS.

Some of these tools still need the Python that comes with QGIS (on Windows, the OSGeo4W Shell), because they run the plugin's own code. The others run with any Python 3 from a checkout of the repository.

Tool What it does Needs QGIS Python? Input Output When to use openalaqs_standalone aircraft Computes the emissions of each aircraft movement (fixed-wing, helicopters; gate, APU and engine start included) with the three calculation methods No (numpy, pandas, pyarrow, shapely, pyproj) Inventory .alaqs (*_out.alaqs) One CSV of per-movement totals; optionally the aircraft AUSTAL sources and emissions (parquet) Movement-by-movement tables, large studies, parallel runs, checks against the plugin openalaqs_standalone austal Builds AUSTAL-ready inputs for the whole study: stationary sources from the emission factors stored in the study, aircraft optionally No (as above) Inventory .alaqs whose road and parking emission factors were written by the plugin Six folders: sources, emissions (parquet and one GeoPackage per pollutant), receptors, meteo, config, empty AUSTAL folder Dispersion inputs for a full year or a time window, in a pipeline without QGIS scripts/emissions_austal (beta) Runs the plugin's emission calculation without opening the QGIS window, and optionally writes the AUSTAL input files Yes (imports the QGIS libraries) Inventory .alaqs and a key=value config file Emissions CSV, GeoJSON with QML style, AUSTAL input files The plugin's own results for all source types, in batch from the OSGeo4W Shell scripts/austal_from_csv (beta) Writes AUSTAL input files from emissions already computed, and can start AUSTAL Yes (imports the QGIS libraries) Emissions CSV (plugin table, by source view), meteo CSV, grid definition austal.txt, series.dmna, one emission grid file per source group and time step New AUSTAL inputs with another grid or quality level, without recomputing emissions scripts/metar_to_alaqs_meteo.py Converts METAR weather reports into the plugin's hourly meteorology file, with optional stability classification No (standard library only) METAR text, IEM ASOS CSV or Ogimet text meteo.csv (and optional HTML plots) Building the meteorology file of a study from airport weather reports scripts/migrate_alaqs.py Upgrades a study file to the current schema; optionally refreshes reference tables No (standard library only) .alaqs from an earlier version The same file, upgraded in place, with a backup copy Opening a study made with an earlier version (see UPGRADING.md) scripts/migrate_alaqs_gui.py A window with the options of migrate_alaqs.py No, but needs PyQt5 (the QGIS Python has it) As migrate_alaqs.py As migrate_alaqs.py As migrate_alaqs.py, when you prefer a window to the command line scripts/import_engine_test_events.py Loads engine run-up events into a study, with a dry run that checks every row first No (standard library only) Project .alaqs with test-site area sources, and an events CSV (format) Rows in the study's engine test events table Many events at once, or events kept in a spreadsheet log gse_application Assigns ground support equipment to movement categories and computes their emissions Yes (imports the QGIS libraries) GSE list (CSV or .alaqs) and movements (CSV or .alaqs) Gate emission profiles as CSV, or written into the gate profiles table of the .alaqs Preparing study-specific gate (GSE) emission profiles

"Needs QGIS Python" was checked against the imports of each tool. None of these tools is installed with the plugin: get them from a checkout of the repository. openalaqs_standalone, migrate_alaqs.py and import_engine_test_events.py also read files of the plugin folder of that checkout (calculation code, study templates), so run them from the repository root as their pages show.

See also:

  • openalaqs_standalone USAGE.md: install, commands and options of the standalone
  • scripts/README.md: all command-line scripts
  • INPUT_FORMATS.md: the input file formats
  • DISPERSION_AUSTAL.md: running AUSTAL from the plugin

docs.title: Open-ALAQS validation guide
docs.text:
This guide says what to run to validate a new build of the Open-ALAQS plugin and of openalaqs_standalone, and how to judge the results. It is for maintainers and for the reviewer who signs off a build. What the CAEP14 reference implements, and how to update it, is in CAEP14_VALIDATION.md.

Contents:

  • Validation targets
  • What the user brings
  • V1 - Plugin vs reference workbook (training example)
  • V2 - Standalone vs pinned plugin outputs
  • V3 - Plugin, new vs prior build (campaign study)
  • V4 - Standalone on the campaign study
  • V5 - Plugin vs standalone on the same study
  • Tolerances
  • Failure triage
  • Data shipped with this package
  • Companion code
  • Running the automated tests
  • Submission template

docs.title: Validation targets
docs.text:
Two reference targets:

  • CAEP14: the EUROCONTROL training study shipped in this package (example/training/; its 15-movement variant training_v3.alaqs in openalaqs_standalone/validation/data/), computed with the CAEP/ICAO method by the CAEP14 reference implementation. Tests that the calculation primitives agree to float64 noise.
  • A real-airport campaign: a multi-runway, multi-hundred-movement study the user maintains locally. Tests scale, multi-runway dispatch, and end-to-end AUSTAL prep. This guide refers to it as the campaign study; substitute the filename the user uses (e.g. <study>.alaqs).

The validation matrix:

Training fixture (CAEP14) Campaign study Plugin (QGIS) V1 V3 Standalone (CLI) V2 V4

Plus one cross-check:

  • V5: Standalone vs Plugin on the same study (per-movement diff, both CAEP14 and campaign).

This document is self-contained. Hand it to a reviewer along with the artifacts each validation produces, and the reviewer can perform the comparison and assessment without further context.

docs.title: What the user brings
docs.text:
For each validation the user runs, the reviewer needs four things:

  1. Build identity: metadata.txt version line for the plugin, git commit / archive checksum for the standalone, the exact CLI invocation used, and the QGIS version when applicable.
  2. Inputs used: md5 of the .alaqs file under test, name of the campaign study, time window if any.
  3. Outputs produced: per-movement CSV, per-source CSV, and (for AUSTAL runs) the austal_folder contents.
  4. Environment metadata: OS, Python version, pandas/numpy/pyproj versions (relevant for floating-point reproducibility).

A copy-paste template is at the end of this file under Submission template.

docs.title: V1 - Plugin vs reference workbook (training example)
docs.text: Goal: confirm the plugin's bymode calculation reproduces the CAEP14 reference within the PASS band of Tolerances per pollutant per movement.

docs.title: Inputs (all shipped in this package)
docs.text:
example/training/training.alaqs project file
example/training/training_out.alaqs canonical CAEP14 inventory
example/training/training_movements.csv 13 movements
example/training/training_meteo.csv 75 hourly meteo rows
example/training/training_ads_b_data.csv ADS-B tracks, imported into the inventory (movement 11)
example/training/training_validation_reference.xlsx reference NOx, CO, HC, PM, SO2
 per movement (the plugin's results beside the CAEP14 reference implementation)

docs.title: Procedure (QGIS)
docs.text:
1. Open QGIS 3.40 with the Open-ALAQS plugin installed from the package.
  2. Open example/training/training.alaqs with the plugin's toolbar button Load an Open ALAQS project (QGIS Project > Open does not open an .alaqs).
  3. Open-ALAQS Toolbar > Calculate Emissions Inventory (window Generate Emission Inventory) with the settings of TUTORIAL_ROTTERDAM.md: training_movements.csv for movements, training_meteo.csv for meteorology, training_ads_b_data.csv as ADS-B table, grid 100 x 100 x 20 cells of 250 x 250 x 50 m. Save as training_out_REBUILT.alaqs next to the original so the original is preserved. (Headless equivalent: QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen python3.12 tools/test_fixtures/rebuild_training_example_inventory.py --out example/training/training_out_REBUILT.alaqs.)
  4. Open-ALAQS Toolbar > Visualize Emission Calculation on training_out_REBUILT.alaqs. Method: bymode (default). NOx ambient correction: off (default). Emission Source Type: MovementSource. In the Output Formats tab, set the Emissions table Output view type to by source (the default, by aggregation, gives one total row; by source gives the rows of each movement, which the reviewer sums by source_name).
  5. Click View Emissions Table and export it with Export CSV.

The same export steps (method, NOx correction, by source, Export CSV) apply to every plugin CSV this guide asks for.

docs.title: Outputs to send
docs.text:
• training_out_REBUILT.alaqs (the regenerated inventory), or the md5 if the file is too large.
  • The exported per-movement CSV.
  • The Open-ALAQS log lines from the Visualize Emission Calculation run.

docs.title: What the reviewer does
docs.text:
• Compare the plugin results on training_out_REBUILT.alaqs with those on example/training/training_out.alaqs (the canonical inventory): they must be bit-identical per movement. The files themselves are not md5-identical (a rebuild differs in bytes), so do not md5-compare them.
  • For each movement (13 total), read the plugin CSV and read training_validation_reference.xlsx. Diff per pollutant and report the per-movement deltas in the three tolerance bands. For a quick installation check, compare_inventory_to_reference.py <csv> --method=bymode does this diff against the workbook's reference column with a coarser threshold (see Tolerances).
  • Surface any non-PASS rows in a table, propose root-cause hypotheses (EF table change, profile table change, ambient-correction toggle, meteo expansion); see Failure triage.

docs.title: V2 - Standalone vs pinned plugin outputs
docs.text: Goal: confirm the standalone reproduces the pinned plugin CSVs of the CAEP14 fixture (training_v3.alaqs) within the PASS band (matching method, matching ambient settings). The current build agrees to float64 noise, except bymode with the NOx correction (Current agreement). V2 compares the standalone with these plugin outputs, not with the reference implementation itself; the reference is checked against the same CSVs by compute_caep14_reference.py (CAEP14_VALIDATION.md).

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
The four pinned plugin per-movement CSVs shipped at:

openalaqs_standalone/validation/data/plugin_output/training_movements_bymode.csv
openalaqs_standalone/validation/data/plugin_output/training_movements_bymode_nox_corr.csv
openalaqs_standalone/validation/data/plugin_output/training_movements_bffm2_anchor.csv
openalaqs_standalone/validation/data/plugin_output/training_movements_bffm2_traj.csv

These are pinned plugin outputs used as the comparison target for the standalone. They were generated from the 15-movement training_v3.alaqs fixture (13 fixed-wing + 2 helicopter). Each contains only source_type = "Movement" rows: aircraft trajectory contributions only, with the plugin's separate gate / APU / engine-start source types excluded.

The matching standalone fixture is:

openalaqs_standalone/validation/data/training_v3.alaqs

docs.title: Comparing like with like: --aircraft-only
docs.text: The standalone's per-movement CSV holds the movement total by default (gate, APU and engine start folded in); the pinned plugin CSVs hold the trajectory only. Pass --aircraft-only to the aircraft subcommand to make the two comparable (see USAGE.md). training_v3.alaqs has no gate, APU or engine-start emissions, so on this fixture the flag changes nothing and V2 passes as written; keep it so the procedure also holds on other studies.

docs.title: Procedure (terminal)
docs.text:
From the repository root, with PYTHONPATH=.:

# 1. bymode (default), ambient correction off
python -m openalaqs_standalone aircraft \
 openalaqs_standalone/validation/data/training_v3.alaqs \
 --out v2_bymode.csv --method bymode \
 --aircraft-only

# 2. bymode + NOx ambient correction on
python -m openalaqs_standalone aircraft \
 openalaqs_standalone/validation/data/training_v3.alaqs \
 --out v2_bymode_nox_corr.csv --method bymode \
 --apply-nox-corrections --aircraft-only

# 3. BFFM2 anchor
python -m openalaqs_standalone aircraft \
 openalaqs_standalone/validation/data/training_v3.alaqs \
 --out v2_bffm2_anchor.csv --method bffm2_anchor \
 --aircraft-only

# 4. BFFM2 trajectory
python -m openalaqs_standalone aircraft \
 openalaqs_standalone/validation/data/training_v3.alaqs \
 --out v2_bffm2_traj.csv --method bffm2_traj \
 --aircraft-only

Meteo: the pinned plugin CSVs were made with the study meteo (tbl_InvMeteo), which the plugin applies to the BFFM2 ambient correction and to the NOx correction. The standalone uses it by default (--use-meteo); do not pass --isa-meteo, which puts the BFFM2 methods and the NOx-corrected run off the pinned files (see Effect of the meteo setting).

Expected per-movement aircraft-only totals (sum across 15 movements in training_v3.alaqs: 13 fixed-wing + 2 helicopter, kg):

Method NOx CO HC bymode 29.197 21.812 1.456 bymode + --apply-nox-corrections 27.963 21.812 1.456 bffm2_anchor 27.990 20.908 1.407 bffm2_traj 15.311 21.546 1.409

(Measured with the standalone of this version, default meteo and --aircraft-only, on training_v3.alaqs; equal to the sums of the pinned plugin CSVs. Any drift here for the shipped standalone indicates a regression. For a NEW build of the standalone, drift is expected and is the V2 result.)

If you are running the 13-movement example inventory example/training/training_out.alaqs (no helicopters) as a smoke test, the totals must match the quick smoke test of USAGE.md, with or without --aircraft-only.

docs.title: Outputs to send
docs.text:
• The four v2_*.csv files produced by the standalone (with --aircraft-only).
  • The standalone version string (__version__, the last line of openalaqs_standalone/__init__.py, or git commit / archive md5).

docs.title: What the reviewer does
docs.text:
• For each v2_*.csv, per-movement diff against the matching pinned file at openalaqs_standalone/validation/data/plugin_output/training_movements_*.csv. The rows are keyed differently: the standalone CSV has one row per movement with an oid column; the plugin CSV identifies the movement by the source_name string (id 1: A20N A 24 → G4 2025-12-01 06:05), so take the number after id as the oid and sum the plugin rows of each movement (as openalaqs_standalone/validation/tests/test_plugin_csv_vs_reference.py does). Expected: PASS everywhere; the measured agreement of this version is in Current agreement.
  • Cross-method sanity (no aircraft should produce zero CO, CO2, HC, NOx, SOx or PM10; SOx is fuel × 0.758 g/kg for every movement of this fixture (jet fuel), helicopters included; all 15 movements should appear in each output).
  • Compare the aggregate NOx totals against the expected table above.

docs.title: V3 - Plugin, new vs prior build (campaign study)
docs.text: Goal: confirm the plugin produces stable per-movement outputs on the multi-runway, multi-hundred-movement campaign study the user maintains. There is no independent reference; the new build is compared with the prior validated build, and every row is expected in the PASS band unless a change between the builds explains it.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• <campaign_study>.alaqs: the user's local file, with multi-runway layout, hundreds to thousands of movements, real meteo, real receptors.
  • The previous validated build's per-movement CSV (call it prior_v3.csv).
  • The same user's QGIS project and any per-study tweaks (e.g. tow_ratio overrides in user_aircraft_movements).

docs.title: Procedure (QGIS)
docs.text:
1. Open QGIS 3.40 with the new plugin installed.
  2. Open <campaign_study>.alaqs with the plugin's toolbar button Load an Open ALAQS project.
  3. Open-ALAQS Toolbar > Visualize Emission Calculation on the study's inventory (*_out.alaqs). Run for the inventory year declared in user_study_setup. Method as previously validated (typically bymode).
  4. Export the per-movement table to CSV as in V1 step 4 and 5.

docs.title: Outputs to send
docs.text:
• The per-movement CSV from the new build (call it new_v3.csv).
  • The corresponding prior_v3.csv (user already has this).
  • The metadata.txt version line for the new build.
  • Movement count, total NOx (kg), total CO (kg), total HC (kg) for both runs: a useful sanity check before per-movement comparison.

docs.title: What the reviewer does
docs.text:
• Row-align new_v3.csv and prior_v3.csv by movement oid + direction.
  • Per-movement absolute and relative deltas per pollutant.
  • Summary table: count of rows in each tolerance band.
  • If failures exist, group by aircraft_icao, engine_name, profile_id, and runway to find the dominant pattern.
  • Likely-cause hypotheses, drawing on knowledge of which files changed between the prior and new builds.

docs.title: V4 - Standalone on the campaign study
docs.text: Goal: confirm the standalone produces the same per-movement results as the plugin (V3) on the campaign study, and is unchanged from its own prior-build output for the same input.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• <campaign_study>.alaqs (same file as V3).
  • The standalone build under test.
  • The plugin CSV from V3 (so V5 can also be run from these artifacts).

docs.title: Procedure (terminal)
docs.text:
# aircraft compute only (movement-by-movement totals)
python -m openalaqs_standalone aircraft \
 <campaign_study>.alaqs \
 --out v4_aircraft.csv \
 --method bymode \
 --aircraft-only \
 --processes 8

# full austal pipeline (six folders including aircraft cell sources)
python -m openalaqs_standalone austal \
 <campaign_study>.alaqs \
 --year <year_from_user_study_setup> \
 --include-aircraft --aircraft-method bymode \
 --processes 8 \
 --out ./v4_austal/

--aircraft-only because v4_aircraft.csv is compared with the plugin's Movement rows in V5 (see V2). The flag does not change the austal run.

docs.title: Outputs to send
docs.text:
• v4_aircraft.csv: per-movement aircraft-trajectory totals.
  • v4_austal/emissions_folder/emissions.parquet: hourly per-source rates.
  • v4_austal/config_folder/config.json: write settings, grid, time window.
  • v4_austal/sources_folder/sources.parquet: source geometry + metadata.
  • Standalone version, CLI invocation, walltime, peak memory if known.

docs.title: What the reviewer does
docs.text:
• Compare v4_aircraft.csv against V3's plugin CSV per-movement (per V5 below).
  • Cross-check emissions.parquet aggregates by source type (the source_type of sources.parquet: aircraft, road, parking, point, area, engine_test, gate; gate emissions are folded into the aircraft totals) against per-type totals from V3's plugin run when reported.
  • Verify config.json has the expected keys (apply_nox_corrections, grid.utm_epsg, grid.nx/ny, start_dt/end_dt, selected_pollutants); the keys are listed in USAGE.md.

docs.title: V5 - Plugin vs standalone on the same study
docs.text: Goal: every per-movement row in the plugin's CSV matches the standalone's aircraft CSV within the PASS band, on the same study (both CAEP14 and the campaign). On the CAEP14 fixture the current build agrees to float64 noise, except bymode with the NOx correction.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• For CAEP14: the V1 plugin CSV and a standalone run on the same inventory (aircraft training_out_REBUILT.alaqs --aircraft-only), or the pinned plugin CSVs and the V2 outputs on training_v3.alaqs.
  • For campaign: V3 plugin CSV + V4 standalone aircraft CSV (run with --aircraft-only, see V4).

docs.title: What the reviewer does
docs.text:
• Build the row-aligned diff table keyed by (oid, departure_arrival) (plugin side: the oid is the number after id in source_name; sum the plugin rows of each movement).
  • Report the tolerance bands per pollutant.
  • For CAEP14: expect 100 % PASS. Any row outside is a regression.
  • For campaign: report the band distribution. Investigate any PASS-WITH-DRIFT rows that did not exist in the prior build's V5 result.

docs.title: Tolerances
docs.text: This section is the one place for the tolerance bands and for the measured agreement between the plugin, the standalone and the CAEP14 reference.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text:
This guide uses three terms, from strictest to loosest:

  • Bit-identical: the same IEEE 754 binary64 value; in a CSV, the same value to all digits the CSV keeps (15 to 17 significant digits with repr or %.17g). Used only for the same code on the same input (V1, rebuilt against shipped inventory).
  • Float64 noise: a relative difference of about 1e-10 or less, from a different order of summation or of operations. Two implementations that agree to this level compute the same thing.
  • PASS band: a relative difference of at most 1e-6 (below).

docs.title: Relative tolerance
docs.text: |Δ / max(|ref|, ε)| with ε = 1e-30 (so zero-reference values don't explode). Compute per (movement, pollutant) cell, not aggregated.

docs.title: Tolerance bands
docs.text:
• PASS (≤ 1e-6): the same calculation; differences come from floating-point order or a formula written in a slightly different but equivalent form (for example the NOx correction with the pressure in hPa).
  • PASS-WITH-DRIFT (≤ 1e-4): subtle drift, likely from one of: reordered summation, slightly different interpolation order, or reference-data refresh. Investigate; usually safe.
  • FAIL (> 1e-4): a real difference. Pollutant or movement is responding to a different code path.

The checks shipped with the code use their own, coarser thresholds: test_plugin_csv_vs_reference.py fails above 2e-4 relative (plugin against reference and standalone, 15 movements, the three methods and bymode with the NOx correction), and compare_inventory_to_reference.py flags a movement above 0.5 % (exit code 0 when all movements pass).

docs.title: Current agreement
docs.text:
Measured on this version, largest relative difference per movement and pollutant:

Comparison Fixture Agreement Standalone vs pinned plugin CSVs, three methods (V2) training_v3.alaqs, 15 movements 3.9e-11 Standalone vs pinned plugin CSVs, bymode with NOx correction training_v3.alaqs 2.9e-7 Reference vs plugin, three methods training_v3.alaqs 3.4e-13 (0.00 % on 15 of 15 movements) Reference vs plugin, bymode with NOx correction training_v3.alaqs 3.1e-6 Reference vs plugin, bymode and bffm2_anchor on every movement, bffm2_traj on the ANP movements example/training/training_out.alaqs, 13 movements 3e-13 Reference vs plugin, bffm2_traj on movement 11 (CUSTOM) training_out.alaqs 2.6e-13 Reference vs plugin, bymode with NOx correction training_out.alaqs 1e-6 to 3e-6 on the six departures (largest on movements 10 and 11) Reference vs standalone, helicopters at mixing heights 914.4, 600, 300 and 100 m, with and without a helipad gate training_v3.alaqs 1e-10 Reference vs standalone net of the gate emissions (APU, GSE, engine start, which the reference does not model); measured before the 5.4.1 fuel-flow scaling operational study, 159 movements, 33 engines 7e-10 (bymode), 6.5e-10 (bffm2_anchor), 4e-8 on the CUSTOM movements of bffm2_traj; one ANP departure of bffm2_traj 6e-4 on NOx (0.02 % of its take-off fuel, in an hour with a 400 m mixing height; cause not isolated)

The rows on training_out.alaqs and on the operational study are not part of the test suite.

docs.title: Effect of the meteo setting
docs.text: The pinned plugin CSVs are made with the study meteo. Run at ISA instead (the standalone's --isa-meteo, or the reference without --use-meteo), the largest per-movement NOx difference from the pinned files is 8 % for bymode with the NOx correction, 22 % for bffm2_anchor and 34 % for bffm2_traj. bymode without the correction and the helicopters are unaffected.

docs.title: Per-pollutant aggregate sanity check
docs.text: For each pollutant, sum across all movements in both files; compute the ratio of totals. If the per-row diff is dominated by a small number of movements (e.g. 5 of 1561), the aggregate ratio will be close to 1.0 while the per-row max-delta will be large. Both are useful diagnostics and the reviewer should report both.

docs.title: Failure triage rules
docs.text:
1. One pollutant, all movements affected: likely an EF table refresh (default_aircraft_engine_ei, default_stationary_ef).
  2. All pollutants, one engine family: engine row replaced or its EI numbers updated.
  3. All pollutants, one profile: default_aircraft_profiles row updated.
  4. All pollutants, BFFM2 only: BFFM2 fuel-flow code path regression (twin_quadratic_fit_method.py, bffm2.py).
  5. NOx only, takeoff/climb-out segments only: --apply-nox-corrections flag flipped between runs, or nox_correction_ambient.py changed.
  6. One aircraft type, all movements: default_aircraft.csv row for that ICAO changed (different engine_name or profile_id).

Failures seen in earlier builds, with their symptoms and the code to check, are listed in REGRESSION_PATTERNS.md.

docs.title: Companion code
docs.text:
The validation tools of openalaqs_standalone/validation/tools/ (the reference, the headless plugin re-export, the workbook builder, the workbook diff) are listed in CAEP14_VALIDATION.md. Other code used by these validations:

Code path Use tools/test_fixtures/rebuild_training_example_inventory.py Rebuild example/training/training_out.alaqs from the example inputs openalaqs_standalone/validation/tests/test_plugin_csv_vs_reference.py Plugin = reference = standalone, 15 movements, 2e-4 openalaqs_standalone/validation/tests/test_bffm2_ambient_propagation_regression.py BFFM2 EI regression pytest scripts/migrate_alaqs.py Upgrade a legacy .alaqs to current schema scripts/migrate_alaqs_gui.py Qt5 GUI wrapper around the migration tool

docs.title: Running the automated tests
docs.text:
Run the two suites separately, from the repository root:

QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen python -m pytest --run-slow tests
python -m pytest openalaqs_standalone/validation/tests

Together on one command line, pytest takes openalaqs_standalone/pyproject.toml as its configuration, the repository's conftest.py is not loaded, and --run-slow is not recognised. Slow tests (@pytest.mark.slow, among them tests/test_emission_calculation.py) run only with --run-slow. Calculations run directly on the bundled .alaqs fixtures can write cache tables into them (test_bundled_fixture_hygiene then fails): run ad hoc calculations on copies, keep the test checkout clean, and give pytest a --basetemp with a few GB of space (the plugin suite used 3.5 GB).

docs.title: recipe_config.json parameter reference
docs.text:
The keys of recipe_config.json and the openalaqs_standalone flags they stand for, for users who drive the standalone from an orchestrator such as the Dataiku recipe.

A recipe_config.json file placed next to the .alaqs file is a portable parameter record. Any orchestrator that runs the standalone can read it to drive the run; the file convention exists so the parameters used for a study live alongside the data rather than in a CLI history. Nothing in this repository reads a recipe_config.json: the standalone CLI takes flags only, and the files here are examples for the Dataiku recipe of the Dataiku update package, which reads the file (the recipe is not in this repository). The only code that opens recipe_config.example.json is a test that checks its z0 / d0 / ha defaults (tests/test_site_parameter_defaults.py).

docs.title: Files in this folder
docs.text:
• recipe_config.minimal.json - a short, real example (the 6 most common parameters). Copy this, rename to recipe_config.json, edit values, drop alongside your .alaqs. Done.
  • recipe_config.example.json - the parameters of the CLI table below plus alaqs_filename and clear_output_folders, with each parameter's value followed by a _<name> documentation key explaining what it does. The _-prefixed keys are documentation only; they are ignored at runtime. Use this as a reference, then copy the lines you actually want into your real recipe_config.json.

docs.title: Mapping to the standalone CLI
docs.text:
Every parameter in this file corresponds to a CLI flag on the openalaqs_standalone austal subcommand (a few also on the aircraft subcommand: --processes, --source-dynamics, --apply-nox-corrections, with --method and --isa-meteo in place of --aircraft-method and --use-isa-meteo):

recipe_config.json key CLI flag year --year include_aircraft --include-aircraft aircraft_method --aircraft-method use_isa_meteo --use-isa-meteo atmosphere_model --atmosphere-model (5.4.1) z0 / d0 / ha --z0 / --d0 / --ha (AUSTAL config and atmosphere aloft; defaults z0 0.1 m, d0 6 z0, ha 10 m + d0, derived when null) apply_nox_corrections --apply-nox-corrections source_dynamics --source-dynamics pollutants --pollutants start / end --start / --end processes --processes meteo_year_shift --meteo-year-shift receptor_source_epsg --receptor-source-epsg receptor_target_epsg --receptor-target-epsg receptor_name_col --receptor-name-col receptor_x_col --receptor-x-col receptor_y_col --receptor-y-col title --title qs --qs grid_size --grid-size (receptor clipping only: cells per side of the square around the grid reference; default the study grid, grid_3d_definition x_cells) grid_step --grid-step (receptor clipping only: cell size in m; default the study grid, grid_3d_definition x_resolution)

grid_size and grid_step do not change the AUSTAL grid, which always comes from grid_3d_definition.

The austal flags --grid-writer-mode (default hybrid), --meteo-input and --receptor-input have no key in this file. The Dataiku recipe of the Dataiku update package reads three more keys that are not in it: grid_writer_mode, tag_outputs and alaqs_names (the last two are described in the recipe's header).

Two keys have no CLI equivalent and are honoured only by external orchestrators that manage their own input / output staging:

Key What it does alaqs_filename Picks one .alaqs from a folder containing several clear_output_folders Empties pre-existing output folders before writing (no-op for the CLI)

Running the standalone from a terminal? Skip the JSON and pass the flags directly (the flags are described in USAGE.md):

python -m openalaqs_standalone austal training_out.alaqs \
 --year 2025 --include-aircraft --aircraft-method bymode \
 --apply-nox-corrections --processes 8 \
 --start 2025-12-01 --end 2025-12-04 \
 --pollutants co,hc,nox,pm10,pm25 \
 --out ./inputs/

See also:

  • openalaqs_standalone USAGE.md: the standalone's commands and options
  • WITHOUT_QGIS.md: which tool to run without the QGIS GUI

docs.text:
Five events on a single test-pad area source (TESTPAD_A), covering both required and optional columns, both twin- and single-engine setups, and implicit- and explicit-engine cases:

Row Aircraft Engine (uid → default) engine_count Modes exercised 1 C25C aircraft default aircraft default (=2) TX, CL 2 PC24 aircraft default aircraft default (=2) TX, AP 3 C25C aircraft default 2 explicit TX, AP, CL 4 PC24 aircraft default 1 explicit TX, AP, CL 5 C25C aircraft default aircraft default (=2) TX, AP, CL, TO

Rows 1, 2, and 5 leave engine_count empty: the compute path falls back to default_aircraft.engine_count for the aircraft type. Rows 3 and 4 show the explicit override.

Every row leaves engine_uid empty; the compute path falls back to the aircraft's default engine (from default_aircraft.engine).

docs.title: How to load
docs.text:
The shipped example/training/training.alaqs already has the engine-test-site schema (shapes_area_sources.is_test_site, the engine_test_events table); an older study needs python scripts/migrate_alaqs.py <study>.alaqs first (from a checkout of the repository; the script is not in the plugin zip).

  1. In QGIS, open example/training/training.alaqs. Create an area source named TESTPAD_A at the desired location, or edit an existing area source and rename its source_id to TESTPAD_A.
  2. Tick the Engine Test Site checkbox on the source form. The rate fields on the Emissions tab and the Profiles combo boxes gray out.
  3. Click Load engine test events CSV.... Browse to this file, review the validation summary (5 valid rows, 0 errors, 0 warnings expected), click Apply.
  4. Save the source form (OK).
  5. Regenerate the emission inventory with a period and meteo that cover the events (for example 2025-01-15 00:00 to 2025-02-04 00:00; the training example's own period, 2025-12-01 to 2025-12-03, contains none of them). In Visualize Emission Calculation, select EngineTestSource and TESTPAD_A to inspect per-hour emissions. Non-zero hours: 2025-01-15 09:00, 2025-01-15 10:00, 2025-01-16 08:00, 2025-02-03 11:00, 2025-02-03 14:00.

docs.title: CSV format
docs.text:
The columns of this file are specified in INPUT_FORMATS.md.

See also:

  • Engine test sites: defining a test site in the plugin
  • Engine test site emissions: how the emissions are computed
  • import_engine_test_events.py: loading events from the command line

docs.title: GSE application
docs.text:
A desktop application to assign Ground Support Equipment (GSE) to aircraft movements and to calculate their emissions, which can be exported as .csv or written back to an OpenALAQS database (.alaqs). This guide is for users who prepare gate (GSE) emission profiles for a study. The application runs with the Python of a QGIS installation (see Installation).

Contents:

  • OpenALAQS description
  • Key components
  • Installation
  • Quick start
  • User guide
  • Main tables
  • Assign GSE window
  • Emissions calculator window
  • Notes
  • Contact and license

docs.title: OpenALAQS description
docs.text:
OpenALAQS is a EUROCONTROL open-source tool designed to model and analyze emissions from aircraft operations and various airport sources. It can calculate emission inventories, visualize data, and perform dispersion modeling with the help of AUSTAL.

It is developed as a plugin for the open-source geographic information system QGIS, simplifying the definition of various airport elements (such as runways, taxiways, and buildings) and enabling the visualization of the spatial distribution of emissions and concentrations. It is fully based on an open architecture, making it easily adaptable to other GIS platforms and databases.

docs.title: Key components
docs.text:
• gse.py - Main application entry point and UI controller (Qt through qgis.PyQt). Loads GSE list, emission standards and movements and exposes the tabs: GSE, Emission Standards and Movements.
  • movement_editor.py - Dialog to assign GSE to movement categories (ac_group / gate_type / arrival-or-departure). Produces assignment objects used by the calculator.
  • emissions_calculator.py - Dialog that calculates emissions from assignments and allows export to .csv or update of an OpenALAQS SQLite database table default_gate_profiles.
  • views/ - Qt Designer generated views (UI layout files and generated Python modules).
  • model/ - Database abstraction layer used to load/save GSE, emission factors and other resources.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The application imports qgis.core and qgis.PyQt (gse.py and the modules it loads), so it must run with the Python interpreter of a QGIS installation, for example from the OSGeo4W Shell on Windows. A plain virtual environment with only requirements.txt installed cannot run it, since qgis is not a pip package.

  1. Open a shell that uses the QGIS Python and check that the QGIS modules can be imported:
python -c "import qgis.core"
  1. Install pandas into that environment if it is missing (requirements.txt lists PyQt5 and pandas; Qt itself is provided by QGIS):
python -m pip install pandas

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
From this folder (i.e. gse_application), in the QGIS Python shell described in Installation, run:

python gse.py

The command opens the main window. The application defaults to using .csv backend files (default_gse.csv inside model/database), but an OpenALAQS database .alaqs file can be opened via the "Open Database" action button in the UI to work directly against a database backend.

docs.title: User guide
docs.text: This User Guide summarises the main application functionality, purpose and behaviour of each feature.

docs.title: Main tables
docs.text:
Below are short descriptions for each main tab/section in the application and what users can do in each one.

  • GSE (Ground Support Equipment)
  • Purpose: This table lists the GSE inventory (type, description, power, load factor, fuel and Stage). It is the list used when assigning equipment to movement categories and when calculating emissions.
  • Editing: Rows can be added, removed or modified directly in the GSE tab. Changes are saved back to the existing GSE source (.csv or .alaqs) when the "Save Changes" button is used. The application updates the underlying backends.
  • Validation / checks: The UI performs basic checks to ensure input validity before saving.

  • Behavioural note: Edits are applied to the in-memory model immediately but are only persisted to disk/database when the user presses "Save Changes"; unsaved edits will be lost if the application exits or a different database is opened without saving.

  • Emission Standards

  • Purpose: Holds the emission factor definitions used to convert GSE power and operating time into emissions (CO, HC, NOx, PM, SOx). The emission factors include fields like stage and power_range and per-kWh emission rates (e.g., CO_g_per_kWh).

  • How they are used: When calculating emissions the app will match the GSE Stage and power range with an emission factor row to compute grams emitted per operation.

  • Movements

  • Purpose: Movements data defines which aircraft groups operate at which gate types and whether the movement is an arrival (A) or departure (D). Calculations aggregate GSE consumption/emissions per movement category (ac_group / gate_type / A|D).
  • Input formats: The application reads movements from the user_aircraft_movements table of an OpenALAQS SQLite database (.alaqs / .db) or from a movements CSV. When a .csv file is chosen with "Open Database", the application does not read that file itself: it looks in the same folder for user_aircraft_movements.csv, then movements.csv, and reads the first one found with ; as the separator.
  • Required columns: the movements CSV, or the user_aircraft_movements table, must contain all 20 movement headers listed in MOVEMENTS_HEADERS in gse.py (runway_time, block_time, aircraft, gate, departure_arrival, runway, engine_name, profile_id, track_id, taxi_route, tow_ratio, apu_code, gate_emissions_code, taxi_engine_count, the three set_time_of_main_engine_... columns, engine_thrust_level_for_taxiing, taxi_fuel_ratio, number_of_stop_and_gos); otherwise a warning lists the missing columns and no movements are loaded. An ac_group column is not accepted in place of aircraft.
  • Editing: Movements are typically edited outside the application (.csv or .alaqs); however, a new movements .csv can be loaded via the "Open Database" action and then the "Assign GSE" flow can be re-run. The Movement Editor dialog allows assigning GSE per movement code and adjusting time, count and deterioration factor per assignment.

docs.title: Assign GSE window
docs.text: - Purpose: The Assign GSE window (Movement Editor) presents a list of movement codes (ac_group/gate_type/A|D) and the available GSE list. It allows toggling assignment status and editing the time, count and deterioration factor for each assignment. - Reset vs Modify: When existing assignments are present the dialog prompts to either "Reset" (clear previous assignments and start fresh) or "Modify" (keep existing assignments and allow additions/removals). A "Cancel" option aborts the operation. - Behaviour: Assignments are stored in-memory in the main application until the dialog is accepted and the assignments are merged into the controller state. The movement summary table shows active assignments and their parameters.

docs.title: Emissions calculator window
docs.text: - Purpose: The Emissions Calculator computes emissions from the assigned GSE per movement category. The dialog shows the detailed GSE-by-movement list and the calculated output table with columns for CO, HC, NOx, PM and other fields. - Export options: Calculation results can be exported to: - a new .csv file (via the "Export table to CSV" button), or - the currently opened OpenALAQS SQLite database (the dialog will update the default_gate_profiles table) when the application was opened from a .alaqs / .db file. - Warnings and save prompts: If calculation results exist and were not exported, closing the Emissions Calculator dialog triggers a prompt asking whether to export the results. The prompt offers exporting to .csv or updating the OpenALAQS DB (if applicable); choosing Cancel leaves the dialog open. If an export is performed successfully the dialog closes automatically.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Movement .csv parsing is defensive: missing or empty files will trigger user-facing warnings. The expected columns are defined in gse.py (see MOVEMENTS_HEADERS).
  • When exporting emissions back to the OpenALAQS DB the code will create default_gate_profiles table if missing and will (currently) delete existing rows before inserting the new ones.
  • The doc/GSE-documentation.docx file contains additional details and user guide material. There a more thorough explanation of inputs, formats and examples can be found.

docs.title: Contact and license
docs.text:
This code is part of OpenALAQS. See top-level LICENSE and AMENDMENT_TO_EUPL_license.md for licensing information.

See also:

  • WITHOUT_QGIS.md: which tool to run without the QGIS GUI
  • APU, GSE and engine start: how the plugin uses the gate profiles

docs.title: openalaqs_standalone
docs.text:
The architecture, modules, conventions, limitations and tests of openalaqs_standalone, for developers. To run it, see USAGE.md (install, commands, options, output folders).

openalaqs_standalone is a QGIS-free pipeline that turns an OpenALAQS .alaqs study file into AUSTAL-ready inputs. It covers both source families:

  • Stationary sources (road, parking, point, area): an ALAQS -> AUSTAL adapter. It reads pre-computed emission factors stored in the .alaqs file by a prior OpenALAQS plugin run and spreads them across the year using activity profiles. It does not run COPERT5 or compute those factors itself. See Prerequisite below.
  • Aircraft sources (fixed-wing movements, helicopters, and the gate GSE/GPU emissions those movements drive): a real emission calculator. It walks each movement's trajectory or taxi route and integrates per-segment fuel, time and emission indices, with three selectable methods. This half is validated against the CAEP14 reference and the pinned plugin outputs (see CAEP14_VALIDATION.md).

The package runs without QGIS, without PyQt, and without a native SpatiaLite extension: it reads the .alaqs SQLite directly and parses geometry BLOBs with shapely.

It ships as a top-level package in the Open-ALAQS repository, as a sibling of the QGIS plugin at open_alaqs/. It imports QGIS-free modules of the plugin tree (open_alaqs.core.tools: BFFM2, MEEM, FOCA, fuel sulphur, UTM and runway placement; open_alaqs.core.interfaces.Emissions), and its pyproject.toml packages openalaqs_standalone only, so it is not usable without the plugin tree: run it from the repository root with the root on PYTHONPATH (see USAGE.md). The AUSTAL writer helpers it depends on live in the sibling austal_prep/ package.

Contents:

  • What it produces
  • Architecture
  • Prerequisite: the stationary EFs must already be in the .alaqs file
  • Conventions
  • Limitations
  • Testing

docs.title: What it produces
docs.text:
Two output shapes, depending on which entry point is used.

The austal command builds the six-folder structure that the austal_prep package consumes (sources, emissions, receptors, meteo, config and an empty AUSTAL folder; the folder tree and file schemas are in USAGE.md). With --include-aircraft, the aircraft movement emissions are folded into the same sources.parquet and emissions.parquet: each occupied inventory grid cell becomes a synthetic aircraft:cell:<ix>_<iy>_<iz> source, so one austal_prep run covers the whole study.

The aircraft command runs the aircraft core directly and writes a per-movement totals CSV (one row per movement, one column per pollutant) and, with --austal-out, the AUSTAL emissions.parquet + sources.parquet pair for the aircraft sources alone.

docs.title: Stationary modules
docs.text:
Per-source-type. Each reads one ALAQS table and produces its slice of emissions.parquet; the EFs are already in the file.

_profiles.py           shared: load and apply hourly/daily/monthly
                       activity profiles; STATIONARY_POLLUTANTS
extract_sources.py     read source geometries from .alaqs
                       (all source types, single output)
compute_road.py        roadway segments -> hourly emissions
compute_parking.py     parking lots    -> hourly emissions
compute_point.py       stationary point sources -> hourly emissions
compute_area.py        area sources    -> hourly emissions

docs.title: Aircraft modules
docs.text:
A real per-movement emission calculator, validated against the CAEP14 reference.

geometry.py            QGIS-free spatial primitives; SpatiaLite WKB
                       blob reader
movements.py           .alaqs database accessors for the aircraft
                       pipeline (movements, runway, taxi routes,
                       engines, gates, gate profiles)
compute_aircraft.py    fixed-wing per-movement emissions, three
                       methods (bymode, bffm2_anchor, bffm2_traj),
                       with per-segment records retained
nox_correction.py      ICCAIA NOx ambient correction (take-off weight
                       ratio, temperature and humidity); off by default (see
                       USAGE.md, "The NOx ambient correction")
compute_helicopter.py  FOCA helicopter per-movement emissions
compute_gate_movements.py  per-movement gate (GSE + GPU) emissions,
                       driven by the movements and default_gate_profiles;
                       folded into each movement's total
compute_apu_movements.py   per-movement APU emissions, folded into each
                       movement's total
compute_start_movements.py per-movement engine-start emissions (departures),
                       folded into each movement's total
source_dynamics.py     smooth-and-shift (--source-dynamics default/sas)
                       spatial apportionment
compute_engine_test.py per-event engine-test-run emissions from the
                       `engine_test_events` table. QGIS-free twin of
                       `EngineTestSourceModule`; same math bit-for-bit.
                       Three thrust modes: `snap` (default), `meem`
                       (numerically identical to snap for engine-test
                       events at anchor thrust), `bffm2` (gas-phase
                       ambient correction, PM10/SOx passthrough).
                       BFFM2 requires an optional `conn` kwarg for
                       `tbl_InvMeteo` lookups; snap-only workflows use
                       the same signature as before.
extract_engine_test_events.py  read engine_test_events joined against
                       shapes_area_sources (test-site filter);
                       produces the event-dict input that
                       compute_engine_test.py consumes.
compute_movements.py   dispatch + study-level driver
parallel.py            multiprocessing driver for the movement
                       compute; results bit-identical to the serial
                       driver

docs.title: Distribution and output
docs.text:
distribute.py          per-(time bucket, grid cell) emission
                       distribution: hourly or sub-hour in time, per
                       grid cell in space
austal_aircraft.py     gridded aircraft emissions -> the
                       emissions.parquet + sources.parquet pair
                       austal_prep consumes
inventory_gpkg.py      emissions.parquet + sources.parquet -> plugin-style
                       per-pollutant GeoPackages (<pollutant>_emissions.gpkg)
